 "id": "Q02",
 "sourceFile": "Establishing weighted criteria for return to play after hamstring injury - a systematic review and methodological quality analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "The title in the text, 'Establishing weighted criteria for return to play after hamstring injury: a systematic review and methodological quality analysis', matches the filename, and the article's own printed DOI is 10.1186/s12891-026-10072-z.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "Track & Field", "Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Professional / Elite", "Collegiate", "Adult / Recreational", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "This PRISMA systematic review searched PubMed, SportDiscuss, Web of Science and SciELO on 20 April 2026 for studies on criteria to return to activity after hamstring injury. The text reports 26 included studies (13 primary and 13 secondary reviews) with no pooled analysis, and the authors build a weighted hierarchy of criteria from them. Pain was reported as the most common criterion, with 10 of the 12 studies that addressed it favoring absence of pain, and all 8 studies that analyzed functional tests supporting them.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The included studies are small and of uneven quality (PEDro 3 to 6 of 10 for the three trials in Table 1, STROBE 8 to 19 of 22, PRISMA 2 to 17 of 27), and the weighted hierarchy is the authors' own judgment rather than a validated scoring method. The abstract reports 22 included studies while the results report 26, and Table 4 lists 11 primary studies against 13 in the text.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 10% maximum limb deficit and the weighted criteria hierarchy as validated return-to-play cut-offs, when the review says no consensus exists and a secondary review it cites reports that none of the return criteria have been validated.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2026,
   "citation": "Bru-Ruiz JJ, Pérez-Cruzado D, García-Romero J, Ruiz-Muñoz M, Canca-Sánchez JC, González-Sanchez M. Establishing weighted criteria for return to play after hamstring injury: a systematic review and methodological quality analysis. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2026;27:777.",
   "doi": "10.1186/s12891-026-10072-z",
   "abstract": "The authors searched four databases for studies on criteria to return hamstring-injured athletes to activity and report pain as the most common criterion. They recommend combining pain with strength, flexibility and sport-specific movement at maximum speed. The abstract reports 22 included studies, while the results section reports 26.",
   "tldr": "Pain is still the most common return criterion after hamstring injury, and the authors suggest pairing it with strength and flexibility within about 10% of the uninjured leg, plus sport-specific maximum-speed tests. The included studies are small and uneven in quality, and the authors call for standardized criteria, so use these as a checklist to discuss rather than fixed cut-offs.",
   "methods": "This PRISMA-guided systematic review was registered on OSF, with the searches run on 20 April 2026 and no filters applied beyond five publication languages. Two reviewers screened blind in Rayyan (kappa 0.81, rising to 0.96 after discussion), appraising trials with PEDro, observational studies with STROBE and reviews with PRISMA. The authors then weighted each criterion by evidence level, internal validity and clinical consensus or relapse prediction, and presented the result as a hierarchy diagram.",
   "findings": "Pain was the most common criterion: 10 of the 12 studies that addressed it favored absence of pain and 2 opposed its use. All 8 studies that analyzed functional tests supported them, while imaging was the least favored criterion (3 supported it and 6 opposed it). The authors describe a maximum 10% deficit against the uninjured limb for strength and flexibility as a consensus, drawn from a handful of included studies, and report that De Vos et al. linked pain on palpation at return to almost four times the relapse risk.",
   "limitations": "The authors acknowledge heterogeneous study designs, inconsistent methodological quality and little standardization of instruments and thresholds. The abstract's 22 studies conflicts with the 26 in the results, and the text's 13 primary studies appear as 11 in Table 4. The search used only hamstring terms, although the Strengths section calls it the first review of return criteria for lower-limb injuries, and the weighting is author judgment rather than a validated method.",
   "practicalImplications": "Build return decisions from several measures rather than pain alone, and record the exact instrument and test protocol, which the authors found often unreported. Where pre-injury data are missing, use the uninjured limb as the reference, which the authors describe as the more practical and reproducible option.",
   "athleteDev": "Treat return-to-play testing as a profile of pain, strength, flexibility and maximum-speed or sport-specific movement, each compared with the uninjured leg. The review gives no validated thresholds, so the 10% limb deficit and the 60 m sprint result within 2% of pre-injury (from one 12-athlete sprinter cohort, Otsuka et al. 2022) should be starting points for local data, not cut-offs.",
   "rtp": "The review supports using pain, limb-to-limb strength and flexibility, and functional tests together when deciding return to sport after hamstring injury. It cannot set a validated cut-off or show that any single criterion predicts re-injury: the authors say no consensus exists, a secondary review they cite reports that none of the return criteria have been validated, and the relapse risk estimates, such as about 4% higher relapse risk per newton of strength lost, come from one 64-patient trial (De Vos et al. 2014)."
 }
}

Establishing weighted criteria for return
to play after hamstring injury: a systematic
review and methodological quality analysis
Juan Javier Bru-Ruiz1, David Pérez-Cruzado1,2* , Jerónimo García-Romero3, María Ruiz-Muñoz4,
José Carlos Canca-Sánchez4,5 and Manuel González-Sanchez1,2
Abstract
Introduction Hamstring injuries are the most prevalent in active individuals aged between 20 and 70 years, with
a high recurrence rate of 57% during the first month. The lack of a clear consensus on the return to activity of these
patients could lead to an increase in the incidence of relapses, as well as greater economic costs.
Methods A systematic review was carried out, following the PRISMA guidelines. The article search was conducted
in the PubMed, Sportdiscuss, WOS and Scielo databases, using the terms “hamstring muscle” OR “biceps femoris” OR
“semimembranosus” OR “semitendinosus” OR “hamstring tendon” OR “semitendinosus tendon” OR “semimembranosus
tendon” OR “biceps femoris tendon” AND “return to sport” OR “return to play” OR “resumption of sporting activities” OR
“return to sporting activities” OR “recreational activities resumption” OR “return to recreational activities”.
Results 22 studies were finally included in the present review. The main variables analyzed were the presence of
pain, the performance of functional tests, the measurement of flexibility and range of motion, the strength developed
and the use of imaging tests.
Conclusion Pain measurement has been shown to be the most common criterion for determining return to activity,
and its combination with other complementary measurements such as strength, flexibility and the ability to perform
sport-specific movements at maximum speed is recommended.

Discussion
The present systematic review aimed to analyze the tests
to determine the return to activity after a hamstring
injury. This wide range of variables described requires
that a wide variety of articles be analyzed, in order to
reach all the scientific literature published to date and
thus be able to obtain conclusive results in this review. In
the existing literature, it was observed that the variables
of pain, flexibility and range of motion, functional tests
and strength were the most studied and the most fre-
quently used as criteria for returning to activity. At the
same time, the variability in the existing tests and in the
parameters applied to them hinders analyses and com-
parisons in this field of study.

and trunk alignment; cross-study exploratory comparisons by sex did not iden-
tify any results that remained consistently significant after multiple-comparison
correction.
Conclusion: Existing video-analysis evidence from football matches shows that
HSI occurs more commonly in situations without external contact, and that

sprint-type HSI is more frequent than mixed-type HSI; however, the relative
differences between offensive and defensive phases and between the first and
second halves remain unclear. These findings may provide a basis for hypotheses
in football HSI prevention research, suggesting that future studies may consider
examining non-contact injury scenarios in the context of high-speed running,
eccentric load tolerance, and neuromuscular control during the single-leg sup-
port phase; however, the existing video-analysis evidence itself cannot directly
demonstrate the preventive effects of specific training strategies. The above con-
clusions are limited by factors such as the small number of included studies,
inconsistent definitions of injury mechanisms, and insufficient standardization of
video analysis, and future research should further accumulate cross-sex samples
and harmonize reporting standards.

{
 "id": "Q04",
 "sourceFile": "Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football - a systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text matches the filename ('Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football: a systematic review and meta-analysis') and the printed article DOI is 10.1080/07853890.2026.2652116.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Performance", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Collegiate", "Youth / Adolescent", "Adult / Recreational", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) of exercise-based hamstring injury prevention in football participants, compared with usual practice or standard warm-up. Programmes reduced hamstring strain risk (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.71; I2 57%), with a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18 to 1.40). The authors report the benefit was concentrated in high-adherence implementations (RR 0.36 at 75% or more adherence vs RR 0.92 below 75%), and rate the certainty of evidence as low.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Adherence and dose were defined inconsistently across trials, and the adherence finding comes from study-level meta-regression across 14 trials, which cannot establish individual-level causality. Eleven of the 15 trials enrolled only male players, so the female and youth evidence is small.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the adherence and dose findings as a proven programme design rule, but the authors describe them as hypothesis-generating and say the evidence cannot rank programme types or components.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2026,
   "citation": "Gu J, Li Y, Wang Y, Zhang Y. Intervention components, training dose, and adherence in exercise-based prevention of hamstring strain injury in football: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Ann Med. 2026;58(1):2652116.",
   "doi": "10.1080/07853890.2026.2652116",
   "abstract": "This meta-analysis pooled 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) of exercise-based hamstring injury prevention in football. Programmes reduced hamstring strain risk, and the effect was largest when players completed at least 75% of prescribed sessions. Programme type and components could not be reliably separated.",
   "tldr": "Exercise-based hamstring prevention roughly halved hamstring strain risk across 15 football trials, but the benefit appeared only when players completed most of the prescribed sessions. The review cannot say which programme type or component works best.",
   "methods": "Six databases were searched to 1 October 2025 (PROSPERO CRD420251246295) for randomised and cluster-randomised trials comparing an exercise-based hamstring prevention programme with usual practice or a standard warm-up in football participants. Random-effects meta-analysis pooled risk ratios, with prespecified subgroup analyses and meta-regression for training dose, adherence and playing level, and quality was judged with RoB 2 and GRADE.",
   "findings": "The overall RR was 0.51 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.71), equal to 38 fewer hamstring injuries per 1000 participants on a control event rate of 7.8% (95% CI 23 to 50 fewer). High adherence (at least 75%) gave RR 0.36 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.48), against RR 0.92 (95% CI 0.68 to 1.23) for low adherence (P for interaction below 0.00001). Meta-regression across 14 trials gave an RR multiplier of 0.83 per 10 percentage points of adherence, while training frequency and weekly volume did not change the effect.",
   "limitations": "Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 57%) with a prediction interval crossing the null, and the subgroup and meta-regression results are study-level and exploratory. The Discussion states that residual heterogeneity falls close to zero after adding adherence, but no residual I2 or tau2 is reported in the Results, so that claim cannot be checked. Trim-and-fill gave an adjusted RR of 0.54 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.75), and the certainty of evidence was rated low.",
   "practicalImplications": "Track session completion for each player, because the benefit was seen only at high adherence (at least 75% of prescribed sessions). Within the 1 to 4 sessions per week and 1 to 60 minutes per week range studied, higher frequency or volume gave no clear extra benefit, so lower-frequency plans can work if they are delivered consistently. The review does not show that one programme type or exercise component is superior to another.",
   "athleteDev": "For performance staff, the practical point is that protection depended on players completing the programme, so completion should be tracked alongside the prescription. The 1 to 4 sessions per week range was not less protective than higher doses in these trials. The review cannot choose between Nordic hamstring, FIFA 11+ or other programme types, and dose metrics differ across trials.",
   "rtp": "This review cannot inform return to sport. It studies prevention in football participants, not injured players, excludes rehabilitation and post-surgical interventions, and reports no return-to-play timing, readiness or post-injury outcomes."
 }
}

92	2.1. Methodology and literature search strategy
93	This meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251246295) and reported in accordance with
94	the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [28]. A completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided as Supplementary
95	File 1. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, the
96	Cochrane Library, EBSCOhost-SportDiscus, and EMBASE from database inception. The final search was
97	completed on 1 October 2025. Searches were limited to full-text, peer-reviewed journal articles pub-
98	lished in English. The search strategy was developed based on the PICOS (Population, Intervention,
99	Comparison, Outcomes, Study design) framework [29], and the search strategies are provided in the
100	(Supplementary Material Table S1), with any remaining database-specific strategies available on
101	request. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were hand-searched to identify further eligible
102	studies.

104	2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria
105	Randomised controlled or cluster-randomised trials in football participants and other football-related
106	cohorts were eligible if they compared an exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programme with
107	usual practice or a standard warm-up, and reported HSI events as event counts. The referee trial was
108	included; its influence was assessed in sensitivity analyses. HSI was extracted as defined in each trial and
109	analysed as total HSI events (including first-time and recurrent injuries when reported). Usual practice/
110	standard warm-up referred to the team’s routine training and warm-up activities without an additional
111	structured HSI prevention programme. Studies enrolling mixed populations were eligible if football-specific
112	HSI data could be extracted separately.
113	Furthermore, studies were excluded if they used non-randomised designs, evaluated rehabilitation or
114	post-surgical interventions, did not report HSI-specific outcomes (or did not allow extraction of
115	football-specific HSI data), involved non-football cohorts without separable data, or were not available as
116	full-text articles. Reviews, case reports, and animal studies were also excluded.
117	2.3. Data extraction
118	Two reviewers independently extracted data using a prespecified form and entered them into a stan-
119	dardised spreadsheet. Data extraction covered study and participant characteristics (country, sex, age,
120	and playing level) and intervention characteristics (type, duration, session frequency, session duration,
121	and adherence). The population variable distinguished football participants from other football-related
122	cohorts, such as referees. Intervention content was further coded according to predefined components
123	(strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, and flexibility) and by whether the programme incorpo-
124	rated eccentric hamstring training. Then, the programme complexity was classified as single- or
125	dual-component versus multicomponent (≥3 components). Discrepancies were resolved by consensus
126	and, when necessary, by adjudication from a third author. The complete extracted dataset is provided in
127	the online supplementary material.
128	2.4. Quality assessment
129	Methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [30], covering five
130	domains: the randomisation process, departures from intended interventions, missing outcome data, out-
131	come measurement, and selection of the reported result. Assessments were completed independently by
132	two reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus and, when necessary, by adjudication from a
133	third author. RoB 2 was applied at the outcome level (HSI) for each trial. Overall risk of bias for each
134	study was determined according to the RoB 2 algorithm (low risk, some concerns, or high risk).
135	2.5. Certainty of the evidence
136	The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment,
137	Development and Evaluation) framework [31], considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, impre-
138	cision, and publication bias, with findings rated as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty.
139	2.6. Data analysis
140	Effect sizes were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and analysed on the
141	log scale. For each study, log RRs and corresponding standard errors were obtained or derived from the
142	reported data in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [32].
143	For studies reporting injury incidence rates, event counts were extracted when available to enable con-
144	sistent RR estimation. For cluster-randomised trials, we used effect estimates as reported in the original
145	publications when available; otherwise, risk ratios were derived from the reported event counts at the
146	study level. For studies with zero events in one arm, a continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to enable
147	 4 J. GU ET AL.
148	estimation of risk ratios. Pooled estimates were obtained using inverse-variance weighting under a
149	random-effects model [33]. Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q and quantified with
150	the I2 statistic. Subsequently, between-study variance (τ2) was estimated, and prediction intervals for the
151	pooled effect were calculated.
152	Prespecified subgroup analyses examined whether effects differed by training dose (intervention period,
153	session frequency, session duration, and weekly training volume), adherence (low <75% vs high ≥75%),
154	and playing level. High adherence was defined as completing ≥75% of prescribed training sessions.
155	Adherence information was extracted from trial reports and standardised as the percentage of prescribed
156	sessions completed (relative to the prescribed number) for analysis at the study level in our subgroup and
157	meta-regression analyses. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed intervention type, specific programme
158	components (strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, flexibility, and eccentric hamstring training), and
159	programme complexity. Programme complexity was defined a priori as single- or dual-component versus
160	multicomponent, with multicomponent programmes comprising three or more components. Studies were
161	excluded from adherence-based analyses when adherence data were unavailable.
162	Random-effects meta-regression was conducted to examine the association between adherence (%)
163	and intervention effects on the logRR scale. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness using leave-one-out
164	procedures and re-estimation under a fixed-effect model. In addition, the primary meta-analysis was
165	repeated excluding studies judged to be at high risk of bias overall. Publication bias was assessed visu-
166	ally using funnel plots and statistically using Egger’s regression and Begg’s rank correlation tests when
167	at least ten studies were available [34,35]. When asymmetry was suggested, the trim-and-fill method was
168	applied.
169	All analyses were conducted in R (v4.4.3) in RStudio, primarily using the meta and metafor packages.
170	3. Results
171	3.1. Literature search results
172	A systematic search of six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and
173	EBSCOhost-SportDiscus) identified 1,481 records. After removing 449 duplicates, 1,032 records were
174	screened at the title and abstract level, of which 968 were excluded (968/1,032; 93.8%). Sixty-four full-text
175	reports were sought; seven could not be obtained (7/64; 10.9%), leaving 57 for eligibility assessment. At
176	full-text review, 46 reports were excluded (46/57; 80.7%) due to no injury outcomes reported (19/46;
177	41.3%), insufficient data for analysis (17/46; 37.0%), or ineligible study design (10/46; 21.7%). Citation
178	searching identified four additional records, all of which met the eligibility criteria (4/4; 100%). In total,
179	15 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (Figure 1).
180	3.2. Characteristics of included studies
181	Fifteen trials were included (Table 1), enrolling football participants aged 13–45 years across ten coun-
182	tries [10,36–50]. Eleven studies included male-only cohorts, and four included female-only cohorts.
183	Competitive level ranged from high school and amateur to semi-professional, professional, collegiate,
184	and elite teams; one study enrolled amateur referees, whereas the remaining trials enrolled football
185	players.
186	Furthermore, the interventions were exercise-based injury prevention protocols integrated into routine
187	training. Programmes evaluated FIFA 11+ (n = 4), the NHE alone (n = 4), NHE with additional components
188	(n = 3), and single trials of balance-board training, plyometric bounding, flywheel training, and a multi-
189	modal programme. Prescribed training dose ranged from 1.5 to 3.5 sessions/week (median 2) over
190	7–43 weeks (median 21). Session duration was reported in 11/15 trials (4–20 min), most commonly around
191	15 min. Adherence was reported in 14/15 trials, ranging from 21% to 100% (median 84%).
192	Across interventions (Table 2), strength elements were present in 14/15 trials and eccentric hamstring
193	training in 12/15. The balance, plyometrics, and flexibility components each appeared in 6/15 trials,
194	whereas the agility/speed components appeared in 5/15. By intervention type, FIFA 11+ accounted for
195	4/15 trials, NHE-focused protocols (including combinations) for 7/15, and other interventions for 4/15.

201	Methodological quality for the 15 included studies was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool (Figure 2).
202	Overall, one study (1/15) was judged to be at low risk of bias, twelve studies (12/15) raised some concerns,
203	and two studies (2/15) were at high risk of bias. Domain-level assessment indicated that deviations from
204	the intended interventions (D2) were the most common issue, raising some concerns in 14 out of 15 stud-
205	ies (14/15). Missing outcome data (D3) raised concerns in three studies (3/15), and selection of the reported
206	result (D5) raised concerns in two studies (2/15). In contrast, the randomisation process (D1) demonstrated
207	high methodological quality across most studies (14/15 at low risk), and measurement of the outcome (D4)
208	was at low risk in most studies (13/15). These limitations, largely related to deviations from intended inter-
209	ventions, may have attenuated the estimated intervention effects.
210	3.4. Evaluation of meta-analysis results
211	3.4.1. Overall effect test
212	A meta-analysis of 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) showed that exercise-based
213	prevention programmes significantly reduced the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI
214	0.36–0.71; p < 0.0001), corresponding to an approximately 49% relative risk reduction (1 − RR).
215	Between-study heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 57%, τ2 = 0.20). The 95% prediction interval ranged
216	from 0.18 to 1.40. It crossed the line of no effect (RR = 1), indicating that the magnitude of benefit might
217	vary across implementation contexts. 14 of the 15 studies had point estimates favouring the intervention
218	(RR < 1), supporting consistency in the direction of the overall effect (Figure 3).

2.3. Data extraction
Two reviewers independently extracted data using a prespecified form and entered them into a stan-
dardised spreadsheet. Data extraction covered study and participant characteristics (country, sex, age,
and playing level) and intervention characteristics (type, duration, session frequency, session duration,
and adherence). The population variable distinguished football participants from other football-related
cohorts, such as referees. Intervention content was further coded according to predefined components
(strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, and flexibility) and by whether the programme incorpo-
rated eccentric hamstring training. Then, the programme complexity was classified as single- or
dual-component versus multicomponent (≥3 components). Discrepancies were resolved by consensus
and, when necessary, by adjudication from a third author. The complete extracted dataset is provided in
the online supplementary material.
2.4. Quality assessment
Methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [30], covering five
domains: the randomisation process, departures from intended interventions, missing outcome data, out-
come measurement, and selection of the reported result. Assessments were completed independently by
two reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus and, when necessary, by adjudication from a
third author. RoB 2 was applied at the outcome level (HSI) for each trial. Overall risk of bias for each
study was determined according to the RoB 2 algorithm (low risk, some concerns, or high risk).
2.5. Certainty of the evidence
The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment,
Development and Evaluation) framework [31], considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, impre-
cision, and publication bias, with findings rated as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty.
2.6. Data analysis
Effect sizes were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and analysed on the
log scale. For each study, log RRs and corresponding standard errors were obtained or derived from the
reported data in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [32].
For studies reporting injury incidence rates, event counts were extracted when available to enable con-
sistent RR estimation. For cluster-randomised trials, we used effect estimates as reported in the original
publications when available; otherwise, risk ratios were derived from the reported event counts at the
study level. For studies with zero events in one arm, a continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to enable
 4 J. GU ET AL.
estimation of risk ratios. Pooled estimates were obtained using inverse-variance weighting under a
random-effects model [33]. Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q and quantified with
the I2 statistic. Subsequently, between-study variance (τ2) was estimated, and prediction intervals for the
pooled effect were calculated.
Prespecified subgroup analyses examined whether effects differed by training dose (intervention period,
session frequency, session duration, and weekly training volume), adherence (low <75% vs high ≥75%),
and playing level. High adherence was defined as completing ≥75% of prescribed training sessions.
Adherence information was extracted from trial reports and standardised as the percentage of prescribed
sessions completed (relative to the prescribed number) for analysis at the study level in our subgroup and
meta-regression analyses. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed intervention type, specific programme
components (strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, flexibility, and eccentric hamstring training), and
programme complexity. Programme complexity was defined a priori as single- or dual-component versus
multicomponent, with multicomponent programmes comprising three or more components. Studies were
excluded from adherence-based analyses when adherence data were unavailable.
Random-effects meta-regression was conducted to examine the association between adherence (%)
and intervention effects on the logRR scale. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness using leave-one-out
procedures and re-estimation under a fixed-effect model. In addition, the primary meta-analysis was
repeated excluding studies judged to be at high risk of bias overall. Publication bias was assessed visu-
ally using funnel plots and statistically using Egger’s regression and Begg’s rank correlation tests when
at least ten studies were available [34,35]. When asymmetry was suggested, the trim-and-fill method was
applied.
All analyses were conducted in R (v4.4.3) in RStudio, primarily using the meta and metafor packages.
3. Results
3.1. Literature search results
A systematic search of six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and
EBSCOhost-SportDiscus) identified 1,481 records. After removing 449 duplicates, 1,032 records were
screened at the title and abstract level, of which 968 were excluded (968/1,032; 93.8%). Sixty-four full-text
reports were sought; seven could not be obtained (7/64; 10.9%), leaving 57 for eligibility assessment. At
full-text review, 46 reports were excluded (46/57; 80.7%) due to no injury outcomes reported (19/46;
41.3%), insufficient data for analysis (17/46; 37.0%), or ineligible study design (10/46; 21.7%). Citation
searching identified four additional records, all of which met the eligibility criteria (4/4; 100%). In total,
15 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (Figure 1).
3.2. Characteristics of included studies
Fifteen trials were included (Table 1), enrolling football participants aged 13–45 years across ten coun-
tries [10,36–50]. Eleven studies included male-only cohorts, and four included female-only cohorts.
Competitive level ranged from high school and amateur to semi-professional, professional, collegiate,
and elite teams; one study enrolled amateur referees, whereas the remaining trials enrolled football
players.
Furthermore, the interventions were exercise-based injury prevention protocols integrated into routine
training. Programmes evaluated FIFA 11+ (n = 4), the NHE alone (n = 4), NHE with additional components
(n = 3), and single trials of balance-board training, plyometric bounding, flywheel training, and a multi-
modal programme. Prescribed training dose ranged from 1.5 to 3.5 sessions/week (median 2) over
7–43 weeks (median 21). Session duration was reported in 11/15 trials (4–20 min), most commonly around
15 min. Adherence was reported in 14/15 trials, ranging from 21% to 100% (median 84%).
Across interventions (Table 2), strength elements were present in 14/15 trials and eccentric hamstring
training in 12/15. The balance, plyometrics, and flexibility components each appeared in 6/15 trials,
whereas the agility/speed components appeared in 5/15. By intervention type, FIFA 11+ accounted for
4/15 trials, NHE-focused protocols (including combinations) for 7/15, and other interventions for 4/15.
  Annals of Medicine 5
Figure 1. PRISMA flow diagram illustrating the study selection process for the systematic review and meta-analysis.
Most interventions were single- or dual-component (10/15), with multicomponent programmes (≥3 com-
ponents) comprising 5/15.
3.3. Risk of bias assessment
Methodological quality for the 15 included studies was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool (Figure 2).
Overall, one study (1/15) was judged to be at low risk of bias, twelve studies (12/15) raised some concerns,
and two studies (2/15) were at high risk of bias. Domain-level assessment indicated that deviations from
the intended interventions (D2) were the most common issue, raising some concerns in 14 out of 15 stud-
ies (14/15). Missing outcome data (D3) raised concerns in three studies (3/15), and selection of the reported
result (D5) raised concerns in two studies (2/15). In contrast, the randomisation process (D1) demonstrated
high methodological quality across most studies (14/15 at low risk), and measurement of the outcome (D4)
was at low risk in most studies (13/15). These limitations, largely related to deviations from intended inter-
ventions, may have attenuated the estimated intervention effects.
3.4. Evaluation of meta-analysis results
3.4.1. Overall effect test
A meta-analysis of 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) showed that exercise-based
prevention programmes significantly reduced the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI
0.36–0.71; p < 0.0001), corresponding to an approximately 49% relative risk reduction (1 − RR).
Between-study heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 57%, τ2 = 0.20). The 95% prediction interval ranged
from 0.18 to 1.40. It crossed the line of no effect (RR = 1), indicating that the magnitude of benefit might
vary across implementation contexts. 14 of the 15 studies had point estimates favouring the intervention
(RR < 1), supporting consistency in the direction of the overall effect (Figure 3).

336	3.4.2. Subgroup analyses stratified by training dose, adherence, and playing level
337	There was no evidence of interaction by dose-related parameters, including training frequency, session

343	In contrast, there was evidence of subgroup differences by intervention duration, adherence, and
344	playing level (P for interaction = 0.04, <0.00001, and 0.02, respectively). Interventions lasting 1–6 months
345	(k = 9) were associated with a reduced HSI risk (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–0.66; p = 0.0001), whereas the
346	7- to 10-month subgroup (k = 6) did not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.54–1.09;
347	p = 0.14).
348	Adherence showed the strongest evidence of effect modification. High adherence (≥75%; k = 10) was
349	associated with a substantial reduction in HSI risk (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48; p < 0.00001), whereas low
350	adherence (<75%; k = 4) showed no clear benefit (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; p = 0.56). According to
351	playing level, the association appeared stronger in elite/semi-professional players (k = 8; RR = 0.38, 95%
352	CI 0.23–0.61; p < 0.0001), whereas the amateur subgroup (k = 7) was not statistically significant (RR = 0.77,
353	95% CI 0.53–1.10; p = 0.15).
354	Given the pronounced effect modification by adherence, additional adherence-stratified analyses were
355	conducted across populations and implementation contexts to assess consistency (Section 3.4.3). Other

398	and intervention effects on the logRR scale (β = −0.0190, 95% CI −0.0272 to −0.0109; p < 0.001). This

412	range 0.33–0.64), with no single trial exerting undue influence on the overall estimate. A fixed-effect

414	ies judged to be at high risk of bias (RR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.38–0.76). Excluding the study that enrolled
415	referees did not materially change the pooled effect or heterogeneity (primary: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–
416	0.71; I2 = 57%; after exclusion: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.72; I2 = 59%) [36]. Omitting Engebretsen et al.

418	tive effect (RR = 0.46, 95% CI 0.33–0.64).
419	3.6. Assessment of publication bias
420	Formal tests provided no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry. Neither Egger’s regression test (p = 0.09) nor
421	Begg’s rank correlation test (p = 0.66) was statistically significant. Trim-and-fill analysis identified and
422	imputed three potentially missing studies; the adjusted pooled estimate was slightly attenuated but
423	remained in the protective direction (unadjusted: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71; adjusted: RR = 0.54, 95%
424	CI 0.39–0.75), suggesting that any small study effect, if present, would have limited impact on the overall
425	conclusion (Figure 4). Overall, the available evidence does not suggest major publication bias, although
426	these tests might be underpowered with a modest number of trials, and minor asymmetry could not be
427	fully excluded.
428	3.7. GRADE assessment of the certainty of evidence
429	Certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. As all included studies were ran-
430	domised trials, initial certainty was high but was downgraded by two levels to low. One level was down-
431	graded for inconsistency due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval that crossed
432	the null, suggesting context-dependent effects. Another level was downgraded for risk of bias because
433	most trials raised some concerns or were at high risk of bias overall, predominantly driven by deviations
434	from intended interventions. No downgrading was applied for indirectness or imprecision because the
435	Figure 4. Funnel plot and trim-and-fill analysis assessing small study effects/publication bias for HSI.
436	  Annals of Medicine 11
437	evidence directly addressed the review question, and the pooled confidence interval excluded the null.
438	Publication bias was not downgraded due to no clear evidence of asymmetry, acknowledging the limited
439	power of these assessments.
440	4. Discussion
441	4.1. Main findings
442	This systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomised controlled trials found that exercise-based
443	prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71,
444	p < 0.0001). By restricting inclusion to football-specific RCTs with HSI as the primary outcome, the present
445	synthesis provides estimates with enhanced specificity for applied football settings.
446	The pooled effect exhibits moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%), and the 95% prediction interval crosses
447	the null (0.18–1.40), indicating that intervention effects may vary substantially across contexts. This vari-
448	ability suggests that real-world effectiveness is likely to differ depending on implementation conditions.
449	Implementation conditions may include how programmes are integrated into routine training, the level
450	of supervision and delivery fidelity, and the extent of sustained adherence and control-group contami-
451	nation. When adherence is included as a covariate in meta-regression, residual heterogeneity is markedly
452	attenuated (approaching zero), suggesting that variation in adherence may explain a substantial propor-
453	tion of between-study differences.
454	The present study extends prior evidence by examining sources of heterogeneity rather than simply
455	estimating average efficacy. Specifically, we quantified the adherence–effect gradient using meta-regression
456	and examined prespecified effect modifiers (training dose, intervention duration, adherence, and playing
457	level), alongside exploratory comparisons of programme type, components, and complexity. Both pre-
458	specified subgroup analyses and meta-regression indicate that study-level adherence was consistently
459	associated with effect magnitude and demonstrate a dose–response pattern (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001). In
460	contrast, training dose and programme type show weaker or inconsistent associations with outcomes.
461	Accordingly, while exercise-based prevention programmes can reduce HSI risk in football, achieving
462	meaningful benefits in practice may be contingent on sustained adherence and favourable implementa-
463	tion conditions. Meanwhile, evidence is insufficient to reliably differentiate programme types or pre-
464	scribed training volumes within the ranges examined.
465	4.2. Training dose, adherence, and effect modifiers
466	The risk of bias assessment identifies deviations from intended interventions as the most common con-
467	cern, suggesting that implementation factors such as adherence, contamination, or dose delivery may
468	have attenuated between-group contrasts and contributed to heterogeneity. Similar implementation-related
469	limitations have been noted in prior hamstring injury prevention reviews [14].
470	4.2.1. Training dose
471	Subgroup analyses by training frequency, session duration, and weekly volume show no statistically sig-
472	nificant differences between dose strata, although point estimates generally favour protection across all
473	dose levels. Specifically, interventions involving 1–2 sessions per week and 3–4 sessions per week are
474	both associated with reduced HSI risk, with no clear advantage for higher-frequency (RR = 0.56 vs 0.45;
475	P for interaction = 0.54). Similarly, weekly volumes of 1–30 and 30–60 min show comparable protective
476	effects (RR = 0.42 vs 0.51; P for interaction = 0.62). A meta-analysis of lower limb injuries reported no
477	effect for once-weekly hamstring eccentric training but a significant reduction for twice-weekly ham-
478	string eccentric training (RR = 1.00 vs 0.60) [51], which may reflect differences in injury outcomes, par-
479	ticipant populations, and intervention implementation across reviews. In contrast, in this study’s
480	football-specific HSI synthesis, both 1–2 and 3–4 sessions/week are similarly protective with no evidence
481	of interaction, supporting the feasibility of lower-frequency prescriptions when adherence is maintained
482	[52]. These findings suggest that, within the dose ranges examined, both lower and higher prescribed
483	 12 J. GU ET AL.
484	doses may be effective provided they are implemented consistently. However, interpretation is limited by
485	inconsistent definitions of dose metrics across trials and by potential discrepancies between the pre-
486	scribed and completed dose, particularly in the context of low adherence. Consequently, given the lim-
487	ited statistical power due to small study numbers, the present data do not support strong inferences
488	regarding optimal dose thresholds.
489	4.2.2. Intervention duration and playing level
490	Shorter interventions (1–6 months) demonstrate statistically significant effects (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–
491	0.66), whereas longer interventions (7–10 months) do not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
492	0.54–1.09), with evidence of subgroup differences (p = 0.04). Similarly, elite and semi-professional popula-
493	tions show stronger effects (RR = 0.38, 95% CI 0.23–0.61) than amateur populations (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
494	0.53–1.10; P for interaction = 0.02). Because adherence emerged as a consistent effect modifier across
495	multiple analyses, these duration and level differences may partly reflect systematic variation in adher-
496	ence over time or across competitive contexts [17]. However, the specific mechanisms underlying these
497	patterns are not directly examined in the included trials, and small study numbers within strata limit
498	definitive interpretation.
499	4.2.3. Adherence
500	Adherence emerges as the most consistent effect modifier. High-adherence trials (≥75%) show substan-
501	tial risk reduction (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48), whereas low-adherence trials (<75%) cross the line of
502	no effect (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; P for interaction < 0.00001). Meta-regression indicates a dose–
503	response relationship between adherence and effect magnitude (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001), corresponding
504	to an RR multiplier of 0.83 per 10-percentage-point increase in adherence. Practically, these findings
505	suggest that meaningful HSI risk reduction is most likely when teams achieve and sustain high adher-
506	ence (≥75% of prescribed sessions), with progressively smaller risk ratios as adherence increases. This
507	pattern is consistent across prespecified subgroup analyses and across extended adherence-stratified
508	analyses in different populations and implementation contexts.
509	Additionally, the findings align with broader evidence suggesting that injury prevention effectiveness
510	increases with adherence [18,26,53]. Alternative explanations cannot be excluded. For example, trials
511	achieving high adherence may also have differed in implementation fidelity, participant motivation, or
512	control-group contamination. These findings should be interpreted as signals of effect modification and
513	sources of heterogeneity rather than definitive causal evidence. Individual-level adherence-outcome data
514	will be required to establish causality.
515	4.2.4. Intervention type and components
516	Exploratory comparisons of intervention types and programme components show no consistent differ-
517	ences. Given limited statistical power, small study numbers, and variability in intervention reporting and
518	delivery, these findings should be interpreted as insufficient evidence to differentiate programme types
519	rather than evidence of equivalence. Future trials should improve specification and reporting of both
520	prescribed content and implementation processes, including adherence, fidelity, and progression, to
521	enable more informative comparisons [27].
522	4.3. Implications for practice
523	The present findings suggest three considerations for implementing exercise-based HSI prevention pro-
524	grammes in football.
525	First, adherence appears to be an important determinant of intervention effectiveness. High-adherence
526	trials demonstrate clear risk reduction, whereas low-adherence trials show attenuated effects [45].
527	Accordingly, routinely monitoring adherence and providing regular feedback within teams is likely a key
528	implementation strategy to support sustained adherence and high-fidelity delivery. Programme selection
529	  Annals of Medicine 13
530	and delivery should therefore account for feasibility and sustainability within the team environment
531	[18,53].
532	Second, training frequency and weekly volume in the ranges examined (1–4 sessions per week;
533	1–60 min per week) are both associated with protective effects, with no clear advantage for higher pre-
534	scribed doses. This does not preclude differences by completed dose, which may deviate from the pre-
535	scribed dose under variable adherence. These findings suggest that programmes can be effective across
536	a range of dose levels, provided they are implemented consistently.
537	Third, shorter intervention durations and elite/semi-professional populations show stronger effects
538	than longer interventions or amateur populations. Given that adherence is the most consistent effect
539	modifier across analyses, these differences may partly reflect variation in adherence over time or across
540	competitive levels [47].
541	4.4. Limitations
542	Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
543	First, moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18–1.40) suggest
544	that effects may vary across contexts, and the pooled estimate reflects an average effect.
545	Second, dose and adherence are inconsistently defined and reported across trials, limiting compara-
546	bility. Several included trials used cluster randomisation, and it was not always clear whether clustering
547	was consistently accounted for in the original trial analyses; if clustering is not accounted for, precision
548	may be overstated. In addition, adherence was extracted from trial reports and may vary in definition
549	and measurement accuracy across studies, which could bias the estimated adherence–effect relationship.
550	Subgroup and meta-regression analyses are conducted at the study level and are susceptible to ecolog-
551	ical bias and confounding; adherence-outcome associations do not establish individual-level causality,
552	and alternative explanations (such as differences in implementation fidelity or participant motivation)
553	cannot be excluded. These analyses are therefore hypothesis-generating rather than causal. Third, sub-
554	group analyses are based on small numbers of studies, and multiple comparisons increase the risk of
555	chance findings; these exploratory results require confirmation.
556	Finally, generalizability is limited because most trials enrolled male players (11/15 male-only), and the
557	small number of female-only trials (4/15) precluded sex-stratified analyses; extrapolation to female foot-
558	ball, youth populations, and other team sports should, therefore, be cautious.
559	4.5. Future research
560	Several priorities for future research emerge from these findings. First, future trials should standardise
561	reporting of training exposure and adherence using consistent definitions and core metrics, including
562	session frequency, duration, progression, and attendance; basic process measures such as execution qual-
563	ity should also be documented to improve interpretability and enable cross-study comparisons. Second,
564	comparative evaluations using head-to-head or factorial designs, with cluster randomisation where
565	appropriate, will help clarify which programme components or combinations are associated with benefit,
566	alongside monitoring of control-group activities to mitigate contamination. Third, adequately powered
567	studies in female football and youth populations, together with pragmatic club-based implementation
568	research, are needed to strengthen external validity and inform scalable delivery strategies.
569	5. Conclusions
570	Exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants.
571	Adherence is consistently associated with effect magnitude across multiple stratifications, with preventive
572	benefit concentrated in high-adherence implementations. Subgroup patterns also suggest differences by
573	intervention duration and playing level. Within the examined prescribed-dose ranges, there was no clear
574	additional advantage of higher-frequency versus lower-frequency prescriptions, nor of higher weekly
575	training time versus lower weekly training time. Evidence remains insufficient to reliably rank programme
576	 14 J. GU ET AL.
577	types or specific component configurations. Accordingly, programme selection should prioritise feasibil-
578	ity, and delivery should prioritise maintaining high adherence and implementation fidelity to maximise
579	reproducible preventive gains.

3.4.2. Subgroup analyses stratified by training dose, adherence, and playing level
There was no evidence of interaction by dose-related parameters, including training frequency, session
duration, and weekly training volume (P for interaction = 0.54, 0.72, and 0.62, respectively; Supplementary
Figure S1). Effect estimates consistently favoured the intervention across dose strata. Effects were
broadly comparable for 1–2 sessions/week (k = 8; RR = 0.56, 95% CI 0.38–0.83) and 3–4 sessions/week
(k = 7; RR = 0.45, 95% CI 0.24–0.84). Similarly, both 1–30 min/week (k = 6; RR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68)
and 30–60 min/week (k = 4; RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.27–0.96) were associated with a lower HSI risk.
In contrast, there was evidence of subgroup differences by intervention duration, adherence, and
playing level (P for interaction = 0.04, <0.00001, and 0.02, respectively). Interventions lasting 1–6 months
(k = 9) were associated with a reduced HSI risk (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–0.66; p = 0.0001), whereas the
7- to 10-month subgroup (k = 6) did not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.54–1.09;
p = 0.14).
Adherence showed the strongest evidence of effect modification. High adherence (≥75%; k = 10) was
associated with a substantial reduction in HSI risk (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48; p < 0.00001), whereas low
adherence (<75%; k = 4) showed no clear benefit (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; p = 0.56). According to
playing level, the association appeared stronger in elite/semi-professional players (k = 8; RR = 0.38, 95%
CI 0.23–0.61; p < 0.0001), whereas the amateur subgroup (k = 7) was not statistically significant (RR = 0.77,
95% CI 0.53–1.10; p = 0.15).
Given the pronounced effect modification by adherence, additional adherence-stratified analyses were
conducted across populations and implementation contexts to assess consistency (Section 3.4.3). Other

3.4.3. Adherence-stratified analyses
Adherence consistently modified intervention effects across populations and contexts (Supplementary
Figure S2). Across strata, the pooled RR under low adherence (<75%) was close to 1 and non-significant:
adults (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23), amateur athletes (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23), male athletes
(RR = 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22), and strength-based interventions (RR = 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22). A
similar pattern was observed for eccentric-based interventions: under low adherence (<75%), the
pooled RR was 0.96 (95% CI 0.70–1.32), whereas under high adherence (≥75%), the pooled RR was
0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.48. By contrast, high adherence (≥75%) was consistently associated with a sub-
stantial and statistically significant reduction in HSI risk across these strata (high-adherence pooled
RRs clustered around 0.34–0.38: adults RR = 0.34, 0.25–0.46; amateurs RR = 0.38, 0.28–0.52; males RR
= 0.35, 0.26–0.47; strength-based interventions RR = 0.36, 0.28–0.48; eccentric-based interventions RR
= 0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.48). The between-adherence subgroup differences were statistically significant
within each stratum (P for interaction < 0.00001 throughout). Some strata might draw on overlap-
ping sets of trials, which could yield identical or near-identical pooled estimates across related
stratifications.

3.4.4. Exploratory subgroup analyses: intervention type, programme components, and complexity
Exploratory subgroup analyses examined whether intervention type and selected programme compo-
nents (or programme complexity) were associated with differential effects on HSI risk. Point estimates
generally favoured the intervention across strata. However, there was no evidence of subgroup differ-
ences for any comparison (all P for interaction > 0.05; Supplementary Figure S3). Given the exploratory
nature of these analyses and the limited number of trials within several strata (as few as k = 3 in some
comparisons, although the eccentric training stratum included k = 12), these findings should not be inter-
preted as evidence of equivalence between programmes.
By intervention type, FIFA 11+ (RR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.29–0.97; k = 4) and NHE-based programmes (RR =
0.46, 0.26–0.84; k = 7) were each associated with significant risk reductions, whereas other interventions
were not (RR = 0.53, 0.24–1.18; k = 4); effects did not differ between intervention types (P for interaction
= 0.94).
In addition, component-based analyses showed no evidence of subgroup differences by inclusion of
balance training (p = 0.37), plyometrics (p = 0.22), agility/speed training (p = 0.69), flexibility training
(p = 0.97), or programme complexity (single/dual vs multicomponent; p = 0.69). For eccentric training, the
stratum including eccentric exercise showed a significant protective association (RR = 0.48, 0.33–0.70;
k = 12), whereas the stratum without eccentric training did not (RR = 0.74, 0.36–1.53; k = 3). Nevertheless,
the between-stratum difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.28).
3.4.5. Meta-regression: adherence as a predictor of intervention effects
One study did not report adherence; therefore, the meta-regression included 14 trials (k = 14).
Random-effects meta-regression showed a significant inverse linear association between adherence (%)
and intervention effects on the logRR scale (β = −0.0190, 95% CI −0.0272 to −0.0109; p < 0.001). This
corresponded to an RR multiplier = 0.83 (95% CI 0.76–0.90) for each 10-percentage-point increase in
adherence, equivalent to an approximate 17% reduction in RR (Supplementary Figure S4a). As this was
an aggregate-level analysis, causal inference requires caution.
This dose–response association was consistent across prespecified subsets. Regression slopes were
similar (β ranging from −0.0178 to −0.0194; all p < 0.001), corresponding to RR multipliers of 0.82–0.84

0.77–0.91), male athletes (k = 10; RR multiplier = 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.90), programmes including a strength
component (k = 13; RR multiplier = 0.83, 95% CI 0.76–0.90), and programmes including eccentric training
(k = 11; RR multiplier = 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.89; Supplementary Figure S4b–e). The close agreement across
subsets was consistent with a stable adherence–effect dose–response relationship.
3.5. Sensitivity analyses of the pooled effect
Leave-one-out analyses showed consistent protective effects after omitting any single study (pooled RR
range 0.33–0.64), with no single trial exerting undue influence on the overall estimate. A fixed-effect
model yielded similar results (RR = 0.55, 95% CI 0.46–0.66). Results were robust to the exclusion of stud-
ies judged to be at high risk of bias (RR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.38–0.76). Excluding the study that enrolled
referees did not materially change the pooled effect or heterogeneity (primary: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–
0.71; I2 = 57%; after exclusion: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.72; I2 = 59%) [36]. Omitting Engebretsen et al.
(2008) produced the largest reduction in heterogeneity (I2 = 48%) while maintaining a significant protec-
tive effect (RR = 0.46, 95% CI 0.33–0.64).
3.6. Assessment of publication bias
Formal tests provided no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry. Neither Egger’s regression test (p = 0.09) nor
Begg’s rank correlation test (p = 0.66) was statistically significant. Trim-and-fill analysis identified and
imputed three potentially missing studies; the adjusted pooled estimate was slightly attenuated but
remained in the protective direction (unadjusted: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71; adjusted: RR = 0.54, 95%
CI 0.39–0.75), suggesting that any small study effect, if present, would have limited impact on the overall
conclusion (Figure 4). Overall, the available evidence does not suggest major publication bias, although
these tests might be underpowered with a modest number of trials, and minor asymmetry could not be
fully excluded.
3.7. GRADE assessment of the certainty of evidence
Certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. As all included studies were ran-
domised trials, initial certainty was high but was downgraded by two levels to low. One level was down-
graded for inconsistency due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval that crossed
the null, suggesting context-dependent effects. Another level was downgraded for risk of bias because
most trials raised some concerns or were at high risk of bias overall, predominantly driven by deviations
from intended interventions. No downgrading was applied for indirectness or imprecision because the

Publication bias was not downgraded due to no clear evidence of asymmetry, acknowledging the limited
power of these assessments.
4. Discussion
4.1. Main findings
This systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomised controlled trials found that exercise-based
prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71,
p < 0.0001). By restricting inclusion to football-specific RCTs with HSI as the primary outcome, the present
synthesis provides estimates with enhanced specificity for applied football settings.
The pooled effect exhibits moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%), and the 95% prediction interval crosses
the null (0.18–1.40), indicating that intervention effects may vary substantially across contexts. This vari-
ability suggests that real-world effectiveness is likely to differ depending on implementation conditions.
Implementation conditions may include how programmes are integrated into routine training, the level
of supervision and delivery fidelity, and the extent of sustained adherence and control-group contami-
nation. When adherence is included as a covariate in meta-regression, residual heterogeneity is markedly
attenuated (approaching zero), suggesting that variation in adherence may explain a substantial propor-
tion of between-study differences.
The present study extends prior evidence by examining sources of heterogeneity rather than simply
estimating average efficacy. Specifically, we quantified the adherence–effect gradient using meta-regression
and examined prespecified effect modifiers (training dose, intervention duration, adherence, and playing
level), alongside exploratory comparisons of programme type, components, and complexity. Both pre-
specified subgroup analyses and meta-regression indicate that study-level adherence was consistently
associated with effect magnitude and demonstrate a dose–response pattern (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001). In
contrast, training dose and programme type show weaker or inconsistent associations with outcomes.
Accordingly, while exercise-based prevention programmes can reduce HSI risk in football, achieving
meaningful benefits in practice may be contingent on sustained adherence and favourable implementa-
tion conditions. Meanwhile, evidence is insufficient to reliably differentiate programme types or pre-
scribed training volumes within the ranges examined.
4.2. Training dose, adherence, and effect modifiers
The risk of bias assessment identifies deviations from intended interventions as the most common con-
cern, suggesting that implementation factors such as adherence, contamination, or dose delivery may
have attenuated between-group contrasts and contributed to heterogeneity. Similar implementation-related
limitations have been noted in prior hamstring injury prevention reviews [14].
4.2.1. Training dose
Subgroup analyses by training frequency, session duration, and weekly volume show no statistically sig-
nificant differences between dose strata, although point estimates generally favour protection across all
dose levels. Specifically, interventions involving 1–2 sessions per week and 3–4 sessions per week are
both associated with reduced HSI risk, with no clear advantage for higher-frequency (RR = 0.56 vs 0.45;
P for interaction = 0.54). Similarly, weekly volumes of 1–30 and 30–60 min show comparable protective
effects (RR = 0.42 vs 0.51; P for interaction = 0.62). A meta-analysis of lower limb injuries reported no
effect for once-weekly hamstring eccentric training but a significant reduction for twice-weekly ham-
string eccentric training (RR = 1.00 vs 0.60) [51], which may reflect differences in injury outcomes, par-
ticipant populations, and intervention implementation across reviews. In contrast, in this study’s
football-specific HSI synthesis, both 1–2 and 3–4 sessions/week are similarly protective with no evidence
of interaction, supporting the feasibility of lower-frequency prescriptions when adherence is maintained
[52]. These findings suggest that, within the dose ranges examined, both lower and higher prescribed

doses may be effective provided they are implemented consistently. However, interpretation is limited by
inconsistent definitions of dose metrics across trials and by potential discrepancies between the pre-
scribed and completed dose, particularly in the context of low adherence. Consequently, given the lim-
ited statistical power due to small study numbers, the present data do not support strong inferences
regarding optimal dose thresholds.
4.2.2. Intervention duration and playing level
Shorter interventions (1–6 months) demonstrate statistically significant effects (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–
0.66), whereas longer interventions (7–10 months) do not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
0.54–1.09), with evidence of subgroup differences (p = 0.04). Similarly, elite and semi-professional popula-
tions show stronger effects (RR = 0.38, 95% CI 0.23–0.61) than amateur populations (RR = 0.77, 95% CI

ence over time or across competitive contexts [17]. However, the specific mechanisms underlying these

4.2.3. Adherence
Adherence emerges as the most consistent effect modifier. High-adherence trials (≥75%) show substan-

response relationship between adherence and effect magnitude (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001), corresponding

suggest that meaningful HSI risk reduction is most likely when teams achieve and sustain high adher-
ence (≥75% of prescribed sessions), with progressively smaller risk ratios as adherence increases. This
pattern is consistent across prespecified subgroup analyses and across extended adherence-stratified

Additionally, the findings align with broader evidence suggesting that injury prevention effectiveness

control-group contamination. These findings should be interpreted as signals of effect modification and
sources of heterogeneity rather than definitive causal evidence. Individual-level adherence-outcome data
will be required to establish causality.
4.2.4. Intervention type and components
Exploratory comparisons of intervention types and programme components show no consistent differ-
ences. Given limited statistical power, small study numbers, and variability in intervention reporting and
delivery, these findings should be interpreted as insufficient evidence to differentiate programme types
rather than evidence of equivalence. Future trials should improve specification and reporting of both
prescribed content and implementation processes, including adherence, fidelity, and progression, to
enable more informative comparisons [27].
4.3. Implications for practice
The present findings suggest three considerations for implementing exercise-based HSI prevention pro-
grammes in football.
First, adherence appears to be an important determinant of intervention effectiveness. High-adherence
trials demonstrate clear risk reduction, whereas low-adherence trials show attenuated effects [45].
Accordingly, routinely monitoring adherence and providing regular feedback within teams is likely a key
implementation strategy to support sustained adherence and high-fidelity delivery. Programme selection

and delivery should therefore account for feasibility and sustainability within the team environment
[18,53].
Second, training frequency and weekly volume in the ranges examined (1–4 sessions per week;
1–60 min per week) are both associated with protective effects, with no clear advantage for higher pre-
scribed doses. This does not preclude differences by completed dose, which may deviate from the pre-
scribed dose under variable adherence. These findings suggest that programmes can be effective across

4.4. Limitations
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18–1.40) suggest

Second, dose and adherence are inconsistently defined and reported across trials, limiting compara-
bility. Several included trials used cluster randomisation, and it was not always clear whether clustering
was consistently accounted for in the original trial analyses; if clustering is not accounted for, precision
may be overstated. In addition, adherence was extracted from trial reports and may vary in definition
and measurement accuracy across studies, which could bias the estimated adherence–effect relationship.
Subgroup and meta-regression analyses are conducted at the study level and are susceptible to ecolog-

and alternative explanations (such as differences in implementation fidelity or participant motivation)
cannot be excluded. These analyses are therefore hypothesis-generating rather than causal. Third, sub-
group analyses are based on small numbers of studies, and multiple comparisons increase the risk of
chance findings; these exploratory results require confirmation.
Finally, generalizability is limited because most trials enrolled male players (11/15 male-only), and the
small number of female-only trials (4/15) precluded sex-stratified analyses; extrapolation to female foot-
ball, youth populations, and other team sports should, therefore, be cautious.
4.5. Future research
Several priorities for future research emerge from these findings. First, future trials should standardise
reporting of training exposure and adherence using consistent definitions and core metrics, including
session frequency, duration, progression, and attendance; basic process measures such as execution qual-
ity should also be documented to improve interpretability and enable cross-study comparisons. Second,

appropriate, will help clarify which programme components or combinations are associated with benefit,
alongside monitoring of control-group activities to mitigate contamination. Third, adequately powered
studies in female football and youth populations, together with pragmatic club-based implementation
research, are needed to strengthen external validity and inform scalable delivery strategies.
5. Conclusions
Exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants.
Adherence is consistently associated with effect magnitude across multiple stratifications, with preventive
benefit concentrated in high-adherence implementations. Subgroup patterns also suggest differences by
intervention duration and playing level. Within the examined prescribed-dose ranges, there was no clear
additional advantage of higher-frequency versus lower-frequency prescriptions, nor of higher weekly
training time versus lower weekly training time. Evidence remains insufficient to reliably rank programme
 14 J. GU ET AL.
types or specific component configurations. Accordingly, programme selection should prioritise feasibil-
ity, and delivery should prioritise maintaining high adherence and implementation fidelity to maximise
reproducible preventive gains.

36	1. Introduction
37	Hamstring strain injury (HSI) is among the most frequent non-contact muscle injuries in football (associ-
38	ation football; soccer) and typically occurs during sprinting, rapid deceleration, and cutting actions [1,2].
39	HSIs represent a major burden in professional football, accounting for substantial absence days (approx-
40	imately 25% of all injury-related absences) and requiring meaningful time loss for return to play (mean
41	9 days) [3]. Incidence estimates vary across cohorts and settings, with reports ranging from 1.06 to 5.87
42	injuries per 1000 h of exposure [4]. Surveillance in elite European teams indicates that a greater propor-
43	tion of HSIs occur during match play than training, underscoring their close association with high-intensity
44	game demands [5]. Beyond availability, HSIs impose substantial competitive and economic costs in elite
45	football [3,6].
