54	Recurrence rates of 12–16% within the first year further compound the burden [7,8]. Collectively,
55	these factors position HSI prevention as a practical priority in applied football settings [9–11].
56	Additionally, exercise-based prevention programmes represent the primary approach to HSI preven-
57	tion. Preventive strategies evaluated in football include eccentric strengthening protocols such as the
58	Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE), structured warm-up programmes such as FIFA 11/11+, and multicom-
59	ponent programmes incorporating core stability and balance training [12,13]. Meta-analytic evidence
60	generally supports risk reduction when the NHE is included within prevention programmes, with pooled
61	estimates indicating that hamstring injury rates may be reduced by approximately half [14]. Evidence
62	syntheses also suggest that eccentric resistance training and FIFA 11+ can decrease HSI occurrence in
63	athletic populations, with some meta-analyses reporting reductions of up to 50% [15,16]. However, trans-
64	lation into football practice is complicated by variability in programme content (isolated eccentric train-
65	ing vs multicomponent programmes), prescription (frequency, volume, progression), delivery (integration
66	into routine practice, supervision), and adherence [17–19].
67	Moreover, HSIs are commonly linked to repeated eccentric contractions and high muscular tension
68	demands, supporting eccentric strengthening as a logical preventive target [19,20]. In parallel, modifiable
69	factors such as strength and muscle architecture have been highlighted as key targets for
70	prevention-oriented programming [21,22]. Multicomponent programmes may additionally influence HSI
71	risk by improving movement control and load management during high-speed running and directional
72	changes [23]. Therefore, the present study examines whether preventive effects differ by programme
73	type, constituent elements, training dose, and adherence [9].
74	Despite extensive research, key implementation limitations remain. High-level teams may not adopt
75	HSI prevention protocols consistently, and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is commonly cited as
76	a perceived barrier to the uptake of eccentric-focused exercises such as the NHE, although direct empir-
77	ical evidence linking DOMS to reduced adherence in trials remains limited [17,24,25]. Furthermore, adher-
78	ence appears to meaningfully influence effectiveness, yet has not been consistently quantified across
79	trials and reviews [14,15,18]. For example, fewer than 15% of teams have been reported to complete the
80	recommended FIFA 11+ volume, which may compromise real-world effectiveness [26]. Additionally, meth-
81	odological critiques have questioned the certainty of some large effect estimates, suggesting that rec-
82	ommendations may be conditional on study design and analytic choices [27]. These issues collectively
83	reinforce the need for synthesis approaches that explicitly account for programme modality and imple-
84	mentation factors, particularly adherence and dose.
85	Accordingly, the primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to quantify the
86	association between exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programmes and hamstring strain injury
87	(HSI) risk in football participants. Secondary objectives were to assess whether prescribed training dose,
88	adherence, and playing level modify programme effects. Exploratory analyses compared intervention
89	types, specific programme components, and programme complexity, and meta-regression quantified the
90	adherence–effect association.
91	2. Methods
92	2.1. Methodology and literature search strategy
93	This meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251246295) and reported in accordance with
94	the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [28]. A completed PRISMA 2020 checklist is provided as Supplementary
95	File 1. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, the
96	Cochrane Library, EBSCOhost-SportDiscus, and EMBASE from database inception. The final search was
97	completed on 1 October 2025. Searches were limited to full-text, peer-reviewed journal articles pub-
98	lished in English. The search strategy was developed based on the PICOS (Population, Intervention,
99	Comparison, Outcomes, Study design) framework [29], and the search strategies are provided in the
100	(Supplementary Material Table S1), with any remaining database-specific strategies available on
101	request. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were hand-searched to identify further eligible
102	studies.
103	  Annals of Medicine 3
104	2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria
105	Randomised controlled or cluster-randomised trials in football participants and other football-related
106	cohorts were eligible if they compared an exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programme with
107	usual practice or a standard warm-up, and reported HSI events as event counts. The referee trial was
108	included; its influence was assessed in sensitivity analyses. HSI was extracted as defined in each trial and
109	analysed as total HSI events (including first-time and recurrent injuries when reported). Usual practice/
110	standard warm-up referred to the team’s routine training and warm-up activities without an additional
111	structured HSI prevention programme. Studies enrolling mixed populations were eligible if football-specific
112	HSI data could be extracted separately.
113	Furthermore, studies were excluded if they used non-randomised designs, evaluated rehabilitation or
114	post-surgical interventions, did not report HSI-specific outcomes (or did not allow extraction of
115	football-specific HSI data), involved non-football cohorts without separable data, or were not available as
116	full-text articles. Reviews, case reports, and animal studies were also excluded.
117	2.3. Data extraction
118	Two reviewers independently extracted data using a prespecified form and entered them into a stan-
119	dardised spreadsheet. Data extraction covered study and participant characteristics (country, sex, age,
120	and playing level) and intervention characteristics (type, duration, session frequency, session duration,
121	and adherence). The population variable distinguished football participants from other football-related
122	cohorts, such as referees. Intervention content was further coded according to predefined components
123	(strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, and flexibility) and by whether the programme incorpo-
124	rated eccentric hamstring training. Then, the programme complexity was classified as single- or
125	dual-component versus multicomponent (≥3 components). Discrepancies were resolved by consensus
126	and, when necessary, by adjudication from a third author. The complete extracted dataset is provided in
127	the online supplementary material.
128	2.4. Quality assessment
129	Methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [30], covering five
130	domains: the randomisation process, departures from intended interventions, missing outcome data, out-
131	come measurement, and selection of the reported result. Assessments were completed independently by
132	two reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus and, when necessary, by adjudication from a
133	third author. RoB 2 was applied at the outcome level (HSI) for each trial. Overall risk of bias for each
134	study was determined according to the RoB 2 algorithm (low risk, some concerns, or high risk).
135	2.5. Certainty of the evidence
136	The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment,
137	Development and Evaluation) framework [31], considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, impre-
138	cision, and publication bias, with findings rated as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty.
139	2.6. Data analysis
140	Effect sizes were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and analysed on the
141	log scale. For each study, log RRs and corresponding standard errors were obtained or derived from the
142	reported data in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [32].
143	For studies reporting injury incidence rates, event counts were extracted when available to enable con-
144	sistent RR estimation. For cluster-randomised trials, we used effect estimates as reported in the original
145	publications when available; otherwise, risk ratios were derived from the reported event counts at the
146	study level. For studies with zero events in one arm, a continuity correction of 0.5 was applied to enable
147	 4 J. GU ET AL.
148	estimation of risk ratios. Pooled estimates were obtained using inverse-variance weighting under a
149	random-effects model [33]. Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q and quantified with
150	the I2 statistic. Subsequently, between-study variance (τ2) was estimated, and prediction intervals for the
151	pooled effect were calculated.
152	Prespecified subgroup analyses examined whether effects differed by training dose (intervention period,
153	session frequency, session duration, and weekly training volume), adherence (low <75% vs high ≥75%),
154	and playing level. High adherence was defined as completing ≥75% of prescribed training sessions.
155	Adherence information was extracted from trial reports and standardised as the percentage of prescribed
156	sessions completed (relative to the prescribed number) for analysis at the study level in our subgroup and
157	meta-regression analyses. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed intervention type, specific programme
158	components (strength, balance, plyometrics, agility/speed, flexibility, and eccentric hamstring training), and
159	programme complexity. Programme complexity was defined a priori as single- or dual-component versus
160	multicomponent, with multicomponent programmes comprising three or more components. Studies were
161	excluded from adherence-based analyses when adherence data were unavailable.
162	Random-effects meta-regression was conducted to examine the association between adherence (%)
163	and intervention effects on the logRR scale. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness using leave-one-out
164	procedures and re-estimation under a fixed-effect model. In addition, the primary meta-analysis was
165	repeated excluding studies judged to be at high risk of bias overall. Publication bias was assessed visu-
166	ally using funnel plots and statistically using Egger’s regression and Begg’s rank correlation tests when
167	at least ten studies were available [34,35]. When asymmetry was suggested, the trim-and-fill method was
168	applied.
169	All analyses were conducted in R (v4.4.3) in RStudio, primarily using the meta and metafor packages.
170	3. Results
171	3.1. Literature search results
172	A systematic search of six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and
173	EBSCOhost-SportDiscus) identified 1,481 records. After removing 449 duplicates, 1,032 records were
174	screened at the title and abstract level, of which 968 were excluded (968/1,032; 93.8%). Sixty-four full-text
175	reports were sought; seven could not be obtained (7/64; 10.9%), leaving 57 for eligibility assessment. At
176	full-text review, 46 reports were excluded (46/57; 80.7%) due to no injury outcomes reported (19/46;
177	41.3%), insufficient data for analysis (17/46; 37.0%), or ineligible study design (10/46; 21.7%). Citation
178	searching identified four additional records, all of which met the eligibility criteria (4/4; 100%). In total,
179	15 studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (Figure 1).
180	3.2. Characteristics of included studies
181	Fifteen trials were included (Table 1), enrolling football participants aged 13–45 years across ten coun-
182	tries [10,36–50]. Eleven studies included male-only cohorts, and four included female-only cohorts.
183	Competitive level ranged from high school and amateur to semi-professional, professional, collegiate,
184	and elite teams; one study enrolled amateur referees, whereas the remaining trials enrolled football
185	players.
186	Furthermore, the interventions were exercise-based injury prevention protocols integrated into routine
187	training. Programmes evaluated FIFA 11+ (n = 4), the NHE alone (n = 4), NHE with additional components
188	(n = 3), and single trials of balance-board training, plyometric bounding, flywheel training, and a multi-
189	modal programme. Prescribed training dose ranged from 1.5 to 3.5 sessions/week (median 2) over
190	7–43 weeks (median 21). Session duration was reported in 11/15 trials (4–20 min), most commonly around
191	15 min. Adherence was reported in 14/15 trials, ranging from 21% to 100% (median 84%).
192	Across interventions (Table 2), strength elements were present in 14/15 trials and eccentric hamstring
193	training in 12/15. The balance, plyometrics, and flexibility components each appeared in 6/15 trials,
194	whereas the agility/speed components appeared in 5/15. By intervention type, FIFA 11+ accounted for
195	4/15 trials, NHE-focused protocols (including combinations) for 7/15, and other interventions for 4/15.

198	Most interventions were single- or dual-component (10/15), with multicomponent programmes (≥3 com-
199	ponents) comprising 5/15.
200	3.3. Risk of bias assessment
201	Methodological quality for the 15 included studies was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool (Figure 2).
202	Overall, one study (1/15) was judged to be at low risk of bias, twelve studies (12/15) raised some concerns,
203	and two studies (2/15) were at high risk of bias. Domain-level assessment indicated that deviations from
204	the intended interventions (D2) were the most common issue, raising some concerns in 14 out of 15 stud-
205	ies (14/15). Missing outcome data (D3) raised concerns in three studies (3/15), and selection of the reported
206	result (D5) raised concerns in two studies (2/15). In contrast, the randomisation process (D1) demonstrated
207	high methodological quality across most studies (14/15 at low risk), and measurement of the outcome (D4)
208	was at low risk in most studies (13/15). These limitations, largely related to deviations from intended inter-
209	ventions, may have attenuated the estimated intervention effects.
210	3.4. Evaluation of meta-analysis results
211	3.4.1. Overall effect test
212	A meta-analysis of 15 randomised and cluster-randomised trials (n = 7,465) showed that exercise-based
213	prevention programmes significantly reduced the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI
214	0.36–0.71; p < 0.0001), corresponding to an approximately 49% relative risk reduction (1 − RR).
215	Between-study heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 57%, τ2 = 0.20). The 95% prediction interval ranged
216	from 0.18 to 1.40. It crossed the line of no effect (RR = 1), indicating that the magnitude of benefit might
217	vary across implementation contexts. 14 of the 15 studies had point estimates favouring the intervention
218	(RR < 1), supporting consistency in the direction of the overall effect (Figure 3).

336	3.4.2. Subgroup analyses stratified by training dose, adherence, and playing level
337	There was no evidence of interaction by dose-related parameters, including training frequency, session
338	duration, and weekly training volume (P for interaction = 0.54, 0.72, and 0.62, respectively; Supplementary
339	Figure S1). Effect estimates consistently favoured the intervention across dose strata. Effects were
340	broadly comparable for 1–2 sessions/week (k = 8; RR = 0.56, 95% CI 0.38–0.83) and 3–4 sessions/week
341	(k = 7; RR = 0.45, 95% CI 0.24–0.84). Similarly, both 1–30 min/week (k = 6; RR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68)
342	and 30–60 min/week (k = 4; RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.27–0.96) were associated with a lower HSI risk.
343	In contrast, there was evidence of subgroup differences by intervention duration, adherence, and
344	playing level (P for interaction = 0.04, <0.00001, and 0.02, respectively). Interventions lasting 1–6 months
345	(k = 9) were associated with a reduced HSI risk (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–0.66; p = 0.0001), whereas the
346	7- to 10-month subgroup (k = 6) did not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.54–1.09;
347	p = 0.14).
348	Adherence showed the strongest evidence of effect modification. High adherence (≥75%; k = 10) was
349	associated with a substantial reduction in HSI risk (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48; p < 0.00001), whereas low
350	adherence (<75%; k = 4) showed no clear benefit (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; p = 0.56). According to
351	playing level, the association appeared stronger in elite/semi-professional players (k = 8; RR = 0.38, 95%
352	CI 0.23–0.61; p < 0.0001), whereas the amateur subgroup (k = 7) was not statistically significant (RR = 0.77,
353	95% CI 0.53–1.10; p = 0.15).
354	Given the pronounced effect modification by adherence, additional adherence-stratified analyses were
355	conducted across populations and implementation contexts to assess consistency (Section 3.4.3). Other
356	 8 J. GU ET AL.
357	Figure 2. Risk of bias evaluation conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Collaboration guidelines.
358	subgroup findings, such as those related to intervention duration and playing level, were limited by
359	multiple comparisons and small study numbers in some strata.
360	3.4.3. Adherence-stratified analyses
361	Adherence consistently modified intervention effects across populations and contexts (Supplementary
362	Figure S2). Across strata, the pooled RR under low adherence (<75%) was close to 1 and non-significant:
363	adults (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23), amateur athletes (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23), male athletes
364	(RR = 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22), and strength-based interventions (RR = 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22). A
365	similar pattern was observed for eccentric-based interventions: under low adherence (<75%), the
366	pooled RR was 0.96 (95% CI 0.70–1.32), whereas under high adherence (≥75%), the pooled RR was
367	0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.48. By contrast, high adherence (≥75%) was consistently associated with a sub-
368	stantial and statistically significant reduction in HSI risk across these strata (high-adherence pooled
369	RRs clustered around 0.34–0.38: adults RR = 0.34, 0.25–0.46; amateurs RR = 0.38, 0.28–0.52; males RR
370	= 0.35, 0.26–0.47; strength-based interventions RR = 0.36, 0.28–0.48; eccentric-based interventions RR
371	= 0.36, 95% CI 0.27–0.48). The between-adherence subgroup differences were statistically significant
372	within each stratum (P for interaction < 0.00001 throughout). Some strata might draw on overlap-
373	ping sets of trials, which could yield identical or near-identical pooled estimates across related
374	stratifications.
375	  Annals of Medicine 9
376	Figure 3. Pooled effect of exercise-based prevention programmes on football participants.
377	3.4.4. Exploratory subgroup analyses: intervention type, programme components, and complexity
378	Exploratory subgroup analyses examined whether intervention type and selected programme compo-
379	nents (or programme complexity) were associated with differential effects on HSI risk. Point estimates
380	generally favoured the intervention across strata. However, there was no evidence of subgroup differ-
381	ences for any comparison (all P for interaction > 0.05; Supplementary Figure S3). Given the exploratory
382	nature of these analyses and the limited number of trials within several strata (as few as k = 3 in some
383	comparisons, although the eccentric training stratum included k = 12), these findings should not be inter-
384	preted as evidence of equivalence between programmes.
385	By intervention type, FIFA 11+ (RR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.29–0.97; k = 4) and NHE-based programmes (RR =
386	0.46, 0.26–0.84; k = 7) were each associated with significant risk reductions, whereas other interventions
387	were not (RR = 0.53, 0.24–1.18; k = 4); effects did not differ between intervention types (P for interaction
388	= 0.94).
389	In addition, component-based analyses showed no evidence of subgroup differences by inclusion of
390	balance training (p = 0.37), plyometrics (p = 0.22), agility/speed training (p = 0.69), flexibility training
391	(p = 0.97), or programme complexity (single/dual vs multicomponent; p = 0.69). For eccentric training, the
392	stratum including eccentric exercise showed a significant protective association (RR = 0.48, 0.33–0.70;
393	k = 12), whereas the stratum without eccentric training did not (RR = 0.74, 0.36–1.53; k = 3). Nevertheless,
394	the between-stratum difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.28).
395	3.4.5. Meta-regression: adherence as a predictor of intervention effects
396	One study did not report adherence; therefore, the meta-regression included 14 trials (k = 14).
397	Random-effects meta-regression showed a significant inverse linear association between adherence (%)
398	and intervention effects on the logRR scale (β = −0.0190, 95% CI −0.0272 to −0.0109; p < 0.001). This
399	corresponded to an RR multiplier = 0.83 (95% CI 0.76–0.90) for each 10-percentage-point increase in
400	adherence, equivalent to an approximate 17% reduction in RR (Supplementary Figure S4a). As this was
401	an aggregate-level analysis, causal inference requires caution.
402	This dose–response association was consistent across prespecified subsets. Regression slopes were
403	similar (β ranging from −0.0178 to −0.0194; all p < 0.001), corresponding to RR multipliers of 0.82–0.84
404	 10 J. GU ET AL.
405	per 10-percentage-point increase in adherence: amateur athletes (k = 11; RR multiplier = 0.84, 95% CI
406	0.77–0.91), male athletes (k = 10; RR multiplier = 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.90), programmes including a strength
407	component (k = 13; RR multiplier = 0.83, 95% CI 0.76–0.90), and programmes including eccentric training
408	(k = 11; RR multiplier = 0.82, 95% CI 0.76–0.89; Supplementary Figure S4b–e). The close agreement across
409	subsets was consistent with a stable adherence–effect dose–response relationship.
410	3.5. Sensitivity analyses of the pooled effect
411	Leave-one-out analyses showed consistent protective effects after omitting any single study (pooled RR
412	range 0.33–0.64), with no single trial exerting undue influence on the overall estimate. A fixed-effect
413	model yielded similar results (RR = 0.55, 95% CI 0.46–0.66). Results were robust to the exclusion of stud-
414	ies judged to be at high risk of bias (RR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.38–0.76). Excluding the study that enrolled
415	referees did not materially change the pooled effect or heterogeneity (primary: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–
416	0.71; I2 = 57%; after exclusion: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.72; I2 = 59%) [36]. Omitting Engebretsen et al.
417	(2008) produced the largest reduction in heterogeneity (I2 = 48%) while maintaining a significant protec-
418	tive effect (RR = 0.46, 95% CI 0.33–0.64).
419	3.6. Assessment of publication bias
420	Formal tests provided no evidence of funnel plot asymmetry. Neither Egger’s regression test (p = 0.09) nor
421	Begg’s rank correlation test (p = 0.66) was statistically significant. Trim-and-fill analysis identified and
422	imputed three potentially missing studies; the adjusted pooled estimate was slightly attenuated but
423	remained in the protective direction (unadjusted: RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71; adjusted: RR = 0.54, 95%
424	CI 0.39–0.75), suggesting that any small study effect, if present, would have limited impact on the overall
425	conclusion (Figure 4). Overall, the available evidence does not suggest major publication bias, although
426	these tests might be underpowered with a modest number of trials, and minor asymmetry could not be
427	fully excluded.
428	3.7. GRADE assessment of the certainty of evidence
429	Certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. As all included studies were ran-
430	domised trials, initial certainty was high but was downgraded by two levels to low. One level was down-
431	graded for inconsistency due to moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval that crossed
432	the null, suggesting context-dependent effects. Another level was downgraded for risk of bias because
433	most trials raised some concerns or were at high risk of bias overall, predominantly driven by deviations
434	from intended interventions. No downgrading was applied for indirectness or imprecision because the
435	Figure 4. Funnel plot and trim-and-fill analysis assessing small study effects/publication bias for HSI.
436	  Annals of Medicine 11
437	evidence directly addressed the review question, and the pooled confidence interval excluded the null.
438	Publication bias was not downgraded due to no clear evidence of asymmetry, acknowledging the limited
439	power of these assessments.
440	4. Discussion
441	4.1. Main findings
442	This systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomised controlled trials found that exercise-based
443	prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants (RR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.36–0.71,
444	p < 0.0001). By restricting inclusion to football-specific RCTs with HSI as the primary outcome, the present
445	synthesis provides estimates with enhanced specificity for applied football settings.
446	The pooled effect exhibits moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%), and the 95% prediction interval crosses
447	the null (0.18–1.40), indicating that intervention effects may vary substantially across contexts. This vari-
448	ability suggests that real-world effectiveness is likely to differ depending on implementation conditions.
449	Implementation conditions may include how programmes are integrated into routine training, the level
450	of supervision and delivery fidelity, and the extent of sustained adherence and control-group contami-
451	nation. When adherence is included as a covariate in meta-regression, residual heterogeneity is markedly
452	attenuated (approaching zero), suggesting that variation in adherence may explain a substantial propor-
453	tion of between-study differences.
454	The present study extends prior evidence by examining sources of heterogeneity rather than simply
455	estimating average efficacy. Specifically, we quantified the adherence–effect gradient using meta-regression
456	and examined prespecified effect modifiers (training dose, intervention duration, adherence, and playing
457	level), alongside exploratory comparisons of programme type, components, and complexity. Both pre-
458	specified subgroup analyses and meta-regression indicate that study-level adherence was consistently
459	associated with effect magnitude and demonstrate a dose–response pattern (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001). In
460	contrast, training dose and programme type show weaker or inconsistent associations with outcomes.
461	Accordingly, while exercise-based prevention programmes can reduce HSI risk in football, achieving
462	meaningful benefits in practice may be contingent on sustained adherence and favourable implementa-
463	tion conditions. Meanwhile, evidence is insufficient to reliably differentiate programme types or pre-
464	scribed training volumes within the ranges examined.
465	4.2. Training dose, adherence, and effect modifiers
466	The risk of bias assessment identifies deviations from intended interventions as the most common con-
467	cern, suggesting that implementation factors such as adherence, contamination, or dose delivery may
468	have attenuated between-group contrasts and contributed to heterogeneity. Similar implementation-related
469	limitations have been noted in prior hamstring injury prevention reviews [14].
470	4.2.1. Training dose
471	Subgroup analyses by training frequency, session duration, and weekly volume show no statistically sig-
472	nificant differences between dose strata, although point estimates generally favour protection across all
473	dose levels. Specifically, interventions involving 1–2 sessions per week and 3–4 sessions per week are
474	both associated with reduced HSI risk, with no clear advantage for higher-frequency (RR = 0.56 vs 0.45;
475	P for interaction = 0.54). Similarly, weekly volumes of 1–30 and 30–60 min show comparable protective
476	effects (RR = 0.42 vs 0.51; P for interaction = 0.62). A meta-analysis of lower limb injuries reported no
477	effect for once-weekly hamstring eccentric training but a significant reduction for twice-weekly ham-
478	string eccentric training (RR = 1.00 vs 0.60) [51], which may reflect differences in injury outcomes, par-
479	ticipant populations, and intervention implementation across reviews. In contrast, in this study’s
480	football-specific HSI synthesis, both 1–2 and 3–4 sessions/week are similarly protective with no evidence
481	of interaction, supporting the feasibility of lower-frequency prescriptions when adherence is maintained
482	[52]. These findings suggest that, within the dose ranges examined, both lower and higher prescribed
483	 12 J. GU ET AL.
484	doses may be effective provided they are implemented consistently. However, interpretation is limited by
485	inconsistent definitions of dose metrics across trials and by potential discrepancies between the pre-
486	scribed and completed dose, particularly in the context of low adherence. Consequently, given the lim-
487	ited statistical power due to small study numbers, the present data do not support strong inferences
488	regarding optimal dose thresholds.
489	4.2.2. Intervention duration and playing level
490	Shorter interventions (1–6 months) demonstrate statistically significant effects (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.28–
491	0.66), whereas longer interventions (7–10 months) do not reach statistical significance (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
492	0.54–1.09), with evidence of subgroup differences (p = 0.04). Similarly, elite and semi-professional popula-
493	tions show stronger effects (RR = 0.38, 95% CI 0.23–0.61) than amateur populations (RR = 0.77, 95% CI
494	0.53–1.10; P for interaction = 0.02). Because adherence emerged as a consistent effect modifier across
495	multiple analyses, these duration and level differences may partly reflect systematic variation in adher-
496	ence over time or across competitive contexts [17]. However, the specific mechanisms underlying these
497	patterns are not directly examined in the included trials, and small study numbers within strata limit
498	definitive interpretation.
499	4.2.3. Adherence
500	Adherence emerges as the most consistent effect modifier. High-adherence trials (≥75%) show substan-
501	tial risk reduction (RR = 0.36, 95% CI 0.28–0.48), whereas low-adherence trials (<75%) cross the line of
502	no effect (RR = 0.92, 95% CI 0.68–1.23; P for interaction < 0.00001). Meta-regression indicates a dose–
503	response relationship between adherence and effect magnitude (β = −0.0190, p < 0.001), corresponding
504	to an RR multiplier of 0.83 per 10-percentage-point increase in adherence. Practically, these findings
505	suggest that meaningful HSI risk reduction is most likely when teams achieve and sustain high adher-
506	ence (≥75% of prescribed sessions), with progressively smaller risk ratios as adherence increases. This
507	pattern is consistent across prespecified subgroup analyses and across extended adherence-stratified
508	analyses in different populations and implementation contexts.
509	Additionally, the findings align with broader evidence suggesting that injury prevention effectiveness
510	increases with adherence [18,26,53]. Alternative explanations cannot be excluded. For example, trials
511	achieving high adherence may also have differed in implementation fidelity, participant motivation, or
512	control-group contamination. These findings should be interpreted as signals of effect modification and
513	sources of heterogeneity rather than definitive causal evidence. Individual-level adherence-outcome data
514	will be required to establish causality.
515	4.2.4. Intervention type and components
516	Exploratory comparisons of intervention types and programme components show no consistent differ-
517	ences. Given limited statistical power, small study numbers, and variability in intervention reporting and
518	delivery, these findings should be interpreted as insufficient evidence to differentiate programme types
519	rather than evidence of equivalence. Future trials should improve specification and reporting of both
520	prescribed content and implementation processes, including adherence, fidelity, and progression, to
521	enable more informative comparisons [27].
522	4.3. Implications for practice
523	The present findings suggest three considerations for implementing exercise-based HSI prevention pro-
524	grammes in football.
525	First, adherence appears to be an important determinant of intervention effectiveness. High-adherence
526	trials demonstrate clear risk reduction, whereas low-adherence trials show attenuated effects [45].
527	Accordingly, routinely monitoring adherence and providing regular feedback within teams is likely a key
528	implementation strategy to support sustained adherence and high-fidelity delivery. Programme selection
529	  Annals of Medicine 13
530	and delivery should therefore account for feasibility and sustainability within the team environment
531	[18,53].
532	Second, training frequency and weekly volume in the ranges examined (1–4 sessions per week;
533	1–60 min per week) are both associated with protective effects, with no clear advantage for higher pre-
534	scribed doses. This does not preclude differences by completed dose, which may deviate from the pre-
535	scribed dose under variable adherence. These findings suggest that programmes can be effective across
536	a range of dose levels, provided they are implemented consistently.
537	Third, shorter intervention durations and elite/semi-professional populations show stronger effects
538	than longer interventions or amateur populations. Given that adherence is the most consistent effect
539	modifier across analyses, these differences may partly reflect variation in adherence over time or across
540	competitive levels [47].
541	4.4. Limitations
542	Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
543	First, moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 57%) and a prediction interval crossing the null (0.18–1.40) suggest
544	that effects may vary across contexts, and the pooled estimate reflects an average effect.
545	Second, dose and adherence are inconsistently defined and reported across trials, limiting compara-
546	bility. Several included trials used cluster randomisation, and it was not always clear whether clustering
547	was consistently accounted for in the original trial analyses; if clustering is not accounted for, precision
548	may be overstated. In addition, adherence was extracted from trial reports and may vary in definition
549	and measurement accuracy across studies, which could bias the estimated adherence–effect relationship.
550	Subgroup and meta-regression analyses are conducted at the study level and are susceptible to ecolog-
551	ical bias and confounding; adherence-outcome associations do not establish individual-level causality,
552	and alternative explanations (such as differences in implementation fidelity or participant motivation)
553	cannot be excluded. These analyses are therefore hypothesis-generating rather than causal. Third, sub-
554	group analyses are based on small numbers of studies, and multiple comparisons increase the risk of
555	chance findings; these exploratory results require confirmation.
556	Finally, generalizability is limited because most trials enrolled male players (11/15 male-only), and the
557	small number of female-only trials (4/15) precluded sex-stratified analyses; extrapolation to female foot-
558	ball, youth populations, and other team sports should, therefore, be cautious.
559	4.5. Future research
560	Several priorities for future research emerge from these findings. First, future trials should standardise
561	reporting of training exposure and adherence using consistent definitions and core metrics, including
562	session frequency, duration, progression, and attendance; basic process measures such as execution qual-
563	ity should also be documented to improve interpretability and enable cross-study comparisons. Second,
564	comparative evaluations using head-to-head or factorial designs, with cluster randomisation where
565	appropriate, will help clarify which programme components or combinations are associated with benefit,
566	alongside monitoring of control-group activities to mitigate contamination. Third, adequately powered
567	studies in female football and youth populations, together with pragmatic club-based implementation
568	research, are needed to strengthen external validity and inform scalable delivery strategies.
569	5. Conclusions
570	Exercise-based hamstring injury prevention programmes reduce the risk of HSI in football participants.
571	Adherence is consistently associated with effect magnitude across multiple stratifications, with preventive
572	benefit concentrated in high-adherence implementations. Subgroup patterns also suggest differences by
573	intervention duration and playing level. Within the examined prescribed-dose ranges, there was no clear
574	additional advantage of higher-frequency versus lower-frequency prescriptions, nor of higher weekly
575	training time versus lower weekly training time. Evidence remains insufficient to reliably rank programme
576	 14 J. GU ET AL.
577	types or specific component configurations. Accordingly, programme selection should prioritise feasibil-
578	ity, and delivery should prioritise maintaining high adherence and implementation fidelity to maximise
579	reproducible preventive gains.
580	Acknowledgements
581	The authors would like to express their sincere gratitude to all researchers whose work contributed to this review
582	and meta-analysis.
583	Ethical approval information
584	Not applicable. This study synthesised data from previously published research and did not involve new data collec-
585	tion from human participants.
586	Authors contributions
587	CRediT: Jinfa Gu: Conceptualization, Data curation, Formal analysis, Project administration, Visualization, Writing –
588	original draft, Writing – review & editing; Yan Li: Data curation, Formal analysis, Software, Supervision; Yinhao Wang:
589	Conceptualization, Investigation, Software; Yu Zhang: Formal analysis, Methodology, Validation.
590	Disclosure statement
591	No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.
592	Funding

600	The datasets analysed during the current study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

Outcomes were isometric knee flexor and hip extensor torque, peak eccentric knee flexor torque during NHE, and 0-5, 0-10 and 0-30 m sprint times with FH0, V0 and Pmax, analysed by two-way mixed ANOVA (Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis for NHE eccentric torque).",
   "findings": "Isometric knee flexor torque rose about 11% to 17% in each group, and hip extensor torque rose over time at 0 and 30 degrees hip flexion, all with large or moderate within-group time effects. Sprint times at 0-5, 0-10 and 0-30 m, and FH0, V0 and Pmax, showed no significant time, group or interaction effects.",
   "limitations": "There was no control group without strengthening work, so gains cannot be separated from regular training, and participants and assessors were not blinded. The 35 completers were below the study's own power target of 36.",

   "rtp": "It cannot inform return to sport. Players were healthy (no hamstring injury in the previous 6 months), and the study measured strength and sprint change with no injured group and no rehabilitation or re-injury outcome, so it gives no clearance or readiness criteria."
 }

54	Participants in all 3 intervention groups demonstrated strength increases measure-
55	ments after 4 weeks. Interventions of longer duration or different components should
56	be considered for targeting improvements in sprint performance.
57	Introduction
58	Hamstring strain injuries (HSIs) lead to a high injury burden in male and female
59	football with HSIs leading to 66 days and 57 absent per 1000 hours in collegiate
60	female and elite male Gaelic football respectively [1,2]. Approximately 60% of HSIs
61	occur during high speed running [3]. It is theorised that HSIs occur during terminal
62	swing phase when the hamstrings lengthen actively [4] as the hamstrings experi-
63	ence greater peak lengths and lengthening velocities. During the swing phase, the
64	hamstrings and gluteals produce hip extensor and knee flexor moments, acting in
65	a spring like fashion to slow down the forward momentum at the hip and knee [5],
66	with the combination of hamstrings strength and surface electromyography (EMG)
67	activity during late swing phase significantly contributing to horizontal ground reaction
68	force production [6]. The large biomechanical demands on the hamstring and gluteal
69	muscles indicate their importance in high speed running and performance may, at
70	least partially, explain the observed propensity for hamstring injury during high speed
71	running.
72	Numerous risk factors have been identified including hamstring specific issues
73	such as deficits in isometric, [7] eccentric, [8,9] and endurance [10] strength. Proxi-
74	mal risk factors have also been found; greater gluteal and trunk strength and endur-
75	ance [11] have been observed in those who did not sustain a HSI compared with
76	those who did, while lower isokinetic concentric hip extensor strength was observed
77	in those who subsequently sustained a HSI [9]. In terms of sprinting mechanics, low
78	horizontal force production during in-season testing increased HSI risk in footballers
79	[12]. Consequently, investigating the effects of different interventions on a range of
80	potential risk factors and performance outcomes are needed to refine injury preven-
81	tion programmes [13].
82	The Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) is a knee dominant hamstring exercise
83	found to increase hamstring eccentric strength, improve sprint times and sprint
84	mechanics [13]. Previous studies have demonstrated that short duration NHE
85	interventions of 4 weeks increase hamstring strength [14–16], fascicle length [14],
86	and can improve sprint times [13]. However, research is required to see if other
87	exercises are more effective than NHE interventions [13]. Hip dominant hamstring
88	muscle strengthening exercises, such as the single leg hamstring bridge (SLHB)
89	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529 February 24, 2026 2 / 14
90	 leads to greater surface hamstring and gluteal surface EMG activity compared to the NHE [17], while the razor ham-
91	string curl (RHC) leads to greater peak eccentric knee flexor force that the NHE. [18] However, the effect of these hip
92	dominant exercises on HSI risk factors and sprint performance is not well understood. In addition, the majority of studies
93	investigating the effect of hamstring interventions have been conducted on males, with a specific need to investigate the
94	effects in females. [13,19] Therefore, the research question for this study was to determine the effects of three different
95	hamstring strengthening exercises (NHE, SLHB and RHC) on dominant and non-dominant knee flexor and hip extensor
96	strength measures and sprint performance in female footballers. The objectives were to assess the isometric and eccen-
97	tric knee flexor and isometric hip extensor strength (Newton metres per kilogramme body mass) and sprint performance
98	(split times, maximal horizontal force production [FH0], theoretical velocity [V0], and horizontal power output [Pmax]) before
99	and after a 4 week hamstring strengthening intervention and to compare the effects of the different interventions on the
100	strength and sprint variables. We hypothesised that
101	1. Participants in the 3 intervention groups would demonstrate similar improvements in knee flexor strength measures
102	2. Participants in the hip dominant interventions (SLHB and RHC) would demonstrate greater hip extensor gains com-
103	pared to the NHE
104	3. Participants in the 3 intervention groups would demonstrate improvements in sprint performance.
105	Methods
106	Study design
107	We conducted a randomised controlled trial on female Gaelic footballers from Dublin City University academy to inves-
108	tigate the effects of a 4-week NHE, SLHB or RHC exercise programme on knee flexor and hip extensor strength and
109	measures of sprint mechanics and time. The CONSORT 2010 guidelines for reporting a randomised controlled trial (S1
110	File) were complied with and the trial was registered (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT0573327). An a priori power anal-
111	ysis using G*Power 4.0 (ANOVA: repeated measures, within–between interaction; 3 groups × 5 timepoints) with f = 0.40,
112	α = 0.05, power = 0.80, r = 0.80, and ε = 0.75 indicated a required total sample size of 36 participants. The effect size was
113	informed by meta-analysis standardised mean differences for eccentric hamstring-strength adaptations (0.68–1.11)
114	[20,21]. Volunteers were randomised to the NHE, SLHB or RHC groups by the lead author (EW) using a 6-block randomi-
115	sation pattern (www.sealedenvlope.com). The NHE group were considered to be the control group given that NHE inter-
116	ventions have been repeatedly found to increase eccentric peak knee strength [13]. The participants or the authors who
117	delivered the intervention or assessed the outcomes were not blinded (AC, EH, ST, BB, JK, JT). Evaluations were per-
118	formed before and after the NHE, SLB and RHC programmes in the Athletic Therapy laboratory of Dublin City University.
119	Participants
120	All female collegiate Gaelic footballers (n = 342) at Dublin City University were invited to participate between the 20th of
121	January and 10th of February, 2023. Inclusion criteria were that participants must 18 years or older, free from hamstring
122	injury in the last 6 months, and currently participating in Gaelic football at a varsity level on at least 3 occasions per week.
123	Exclusion criteria included a history of hip or knee injury within the last 3 months, a history of anterior cruciate ligament
124	rupture or involvement in a hamstring strengthening programme within 3 months of the start of the study. The study was
125	approved by the Dublin City University Research Ethics Committee (DCUREC 2022_ATT_EW_15) and written informed
126	consent was provided by all participants. Participants attended two post-intervention sessions between the 27th of March
127	and 5th of April 2023.
128	A familiarisation session and two testing sessions were conducted prior to the intervention from the 13th to 24th of Feb-
129	ruary 2023, with each session separated by 3–5 days. Testing procedures and relevant hamstring strengthening exercises
130	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529 February 24, 2026 3 / 14
131	 were explained and demonstrated. We provided participants with the opportunity to ask questions and practice the testing
132	and exercises with feedback from the investigators where necessary. Participants completed general health and injury
133	questionnaires, and we recorded their body height, mass, chronological age and leg lengths during the familiarization
134	session. Participants were instructed not to commence the exercise programme until the intervention period began. The
135	pre- and post-testing sessions were completed within 6 days of the intervention. Strength assessments were completed
136	on the first day of testing with sprinting performance on the second day.
137	Strength assessment
138	We conducted isometric strength assessment of the knee flexors and hip extensors and eccentric assessment of knee
139	flexor strength during the NHE exercise on participant’s dominant and non-dominant limbs. Isometric assessments were
140	conducted using a microFET®2 Digital Handheld Dynamometer (HHD) (Hoggan Scientific, Salt Lake City, UT) with a
141	sampling frequency of 60 Hz and limb dominance was defined by which leg the participant would prefer to kick a ball with
142	[22]. Participants completed a standardised warm-up on a stationary bicycle ergometer between 80 and 100 rpm for 10
143	minutes followed by two practice repetitions of each at 60% and 80% of maximal effort. Rest intervals of 10 seconds were
144	given between each practice and a 20 second interval between the final practice and maximal test effort. A 1 minute rest
145	was given between each maximal effort test. They were directed to use maximum effort during the maximal effort test and
146	instructed to “Go ahead-push-push-push-push-push and relax”, for each contraction. Each contraction was isometrically
147	resisted by the examiner for approximately 3 seconds during which the tester monitored the HHD display to ensure the
148	reading had plateaued. The highest score of three trials was recorded. We conducted a preliminary intra-tester reliability
149	study that demonstrated a high level of reliability for the strength assessments (ICC 0.89–0.96) (see S2 File).
150	Knee flexor strength was assessed as previously described [23] with the hips in neutral and the knee flexed to 30°,
151	confirmed with use of a goniometer. A ‘break force’ was obtained by pulling down the athlete’s heel to the plinth once the
152	examiner felt the force had peaked and confirmed by monitoring the HHD device (Fig 1). Knee flexor moment arm was
153	by measuring the distance from the lateral femoral epicondyle, which has been shown to represent axis of rotation of the
154	knee joint [24], to 5cm proximal to the lateral malleolus, where the HHD was positioned. Isometric hip extensor testing
155	at 0° hip flexion was completed in prone. A section of the plinth was adjusted to 30° below horizontal so that in prone,
156	participants’ hips were positioned in 30° flexion and the knee flexed to approximately 120° knee flexion (Fig 1). The HHD
157	was positioned on the plantar surface of the calcaneus, directly over the lateral femoral condyle, and the participant was
158	instructed to push their heel up towards the ceiling with the action resisted by the researcher for both tests. Hip extensor
159	Fig 1. Positions for Isometric Strength Testing: A Isometric Knee Flexor Strength, B Isometric Hip.
160	https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529.g001
161	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529 February 24, 2026 4 / 14
162	 moment arm was calculated by measuring the distance from the superior tip of the greater trochanter to the position of
163	the HHD [25], which is this study was directly over the lateral femoral epicondyle. Relative knee flexor and hip extensor
164	peak torque (Nmkg-1) was recorded for each participant [13]. Participants were given a 15-minute break between each set
165	of isometric tests set to minimise the effects of fatigue. Following this, participants were given a 60-minute break before
166	repeating the standardised warm up and completing the NHE knee flexor strength assessment.
167	All NHE assessments were performed on the ‘Hamstring Solo Elite’ (ND Sports Performance, Kilkenny, Ireland) at
168	a sampling frequency of 50 Hz. The device has two separate rigid heel fixators positioned 45 cm above the ground to
169	allow for full knee extension during the NHE, cushioning for the shank which allowed partial glide of the patellae, with
170	the shanks supported at an angle of 30° from horizontal. Participants completed three practice NHE repetitions at 50%,
171	75% and 95% of subjectively rated maximal effort, followed by a 1-minute rest before three maximal repetitions. Partici-
172	pants were requested to maintain their arms across their chest and to lean forwards from the knees, lower their body as
173	slowly as possible (aiming for 4−6 seconds using a metronome at 60 bpm) through as far a range as possible. To facilitate
174	maximal effort, participants were given real time feedback during the NHE. If participants moved into hip flexion or lum-
175	bar lordosis during the test, that repetition was excluded, corrective feedback was given and repeated. We assessed if a
176	participant needed additional resistance by positioning a pole at the participant’s knee at an angle of 20° to assess if the
177	participant was able to control the movement into the final 10−20° of motion [26]. No participants were able to achieve
178	this and therefore additional resistance was not required during testing. Relative peak eccentric torque during NHE testing
179	was recorded (Nmkg-1) [13].
180	Sprint
181	We assessed sprint performance as described by Ishoi et al., 2019 [27] following a standardised and supervised warm-up
182	(FIFA11+) with progressive running and sprinting which lasted approximately 20 minutes. We positioned timing gates
183	with single-beam photoelectric cell systems (Brower TCi Timing Systems, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA) at 0m, 5m, 10m and
184	30m, 2 metres apart from each other. Participants started in a 3-point start position with one hand on a line representing 0
185	metres. The first speed gate was placed at ground level, with the timing gate beam positioned immediately in front of the
186	toes of the back leg. The remaining speed gates were positioned at a height of 100 cm. Each participant performed three
187	maximum effort 30-metre sprints with 2-minutes rest between attempts to minimize the effects of fatigue. The start of the
188	sprint was calculated by using a high speed camera (Canon Legria HF R706, Ota, Tokyo, Japan) to measure the time
189	difference between the initial sprint movement and breaking of the first timing gate. This time was added to sprint and split
190	times to make the corrected times [27]. The fastest corrected time recorded and the corresponding three corrected split
191	times were used to calculate the mechanical sprint variables (maximal horizontal force production [FH0], theoretical velocity
192	[V0], and horizontal power output [Pmax]) using a recognised calculation process [28,29], with FH0, and Pmax normalised to
193	body mass. Based on the best sprint performance, 0–5 m, 0-10m and 0-30m split times (s) and mechanical sprint vari-
194	ables (FH0, V0, Pmax) were recorded.
195	Interventions
196	The NHE [30], RHC [30] and SLHB [10] interventions were completed by participants (see Fig 2, S3 File). If participants
197	were able to control the movement over the last 20° of knee flexion in the NHE or to achieve almost full knee and hip
198	extension for the RHC, additional weight in 2.5 kg increments were added to the exercise to ensure the intensity of the
199	exercise [30], however, this was not necessary.
200	All participants completed a supervised 4-week intervention (Table 1) in the Dublin City University’s Athletic Therapy
201	laboratory. A previous study demonstrated that the number of sets and repetitions and duration of the NHE programme
202	significantly increased eccentric knee flexor peak strength [15], Sessions were supervised by final year athletic therapy and
203	training students who were trained in the interventions by EW, a certified athletic therapist and physiotherapist with more
204	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529 February 24, 2026 5 / 14
205	 Fig 2. Exercise Interventions: A and B start and end position of the Nordic Hamstring Exercise; C and D start and end position of the single
206	leg hamstring bridge exercise; E and F start and end position of the razor hamstring curl.
207	https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529.g002
208	Table 1. Details of the Nordic Hamstring, Single Leg Hamstring Bridge and Razor Hamstring Curl
209	exercise programmes.
210	Week Frequency Sets Repetitions Total repetitions
211	per week*
212	1 2 2 6 24
213	2 2 3 6 36
214	3 2 4 8 64
215	4 2 4 10 80
216	* The number of repetitions are for individual legs for the single leg bridge exercise.
217	https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529.t001
218	than 20 years’ sports medicine experience. We gave participants a recovery time of 10 seconds and 3 minutes between
219	each repetition and set of the NHE and RHC exercises respectively. Participants were given a 30 second recovery between
220	limbs and 3 minutes between sets of the SLHB exercise. Management agreed not to hold lower limb resistance sessions
221	for 48 hours after each intervention session. If a participant was unable to attend a session, they were required to provide
222	video evidence of completion of the appropriate number of exercises within 48 hours of the missed session. Participants
223	had to complete a minimum of 80% of the intervention sessions to be included in the post-intervention assessments, which
224	in practice meant they had to attend for a minimum of seven sessions. Participants were instructed not to complete addi-
225	tional training outside of the interventions and their normal team training programmes and match participation.
226	Statistical analysis
227	Statistical analysis were performed using SPSS (IBM Corp. Released 2021. IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version
228	30.0. Armonk, NY,:IBM Corp). We used the Shapiro-Wilk test to examine for normality and conducted a two-way repeated
229	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529 February 24, 2026 6 / 14
230	 mixed between-within analysis of variance on all data, (with the exception of peak knee flexor torque during the NHE) to
231	examine the interaction and main effects of time (pre vs. post) and group (NHE vs, RC, vs. SLHB) for strength measures
232	of the dominant and non-dominant limbs individually (isometric peak hip extensor torque at 0° and 30° hip flexion, isomet-
233	ric peak knee extensor torque at 30° knee flexion) and performance measures (0-5m, 0-15m, 0−30 m sprint times, FH0,
234	V0, Pmax). As the peak knee flexor torque during NHE data was not normally distributed, we used a Wilcoxon signed rank
235	test to examine the main effect for time and the Kruskal Wallis test to check for main effect of group. Partial eta-squared
236	effect sizes (η2) for interaction effects were classified as small 0.01–0.059; medium 0.06–0.14; and large ≥0.14. [31] If
237	significant group main effects were observed, a Bonferroni post hoc adjustments was made for three comparisons (NHE
238	pre – NHE post, RHC pre – RHC post, and SLHB pre – SLHB post) with a resulting p value of 0.017. Percentage changes
239	after the intervention were calculated for the variable.

303	Discussion
304	This study aimed to investigate the effect of 4-week hamstring strengthening programmes (NHE, SLHB and RHC) on
305	knee flexor and hip extensor strength and sprint performance. We hypothesised that the participants in the 3 intervention
306	groups would demonstrate similar improvements in knee flexor strength measures, those in the hip dominant interventions
307	(SLHB and RHC) would demonstrate greater hip extensor strength gains compared with the NHE and all three groups
308	demonstrate improvements in sprint performance. The results of the study supported the first hypothesis as the partic-
309	ipants in the three groups demonstrated increased post intervention knee flexor isometric and eccentric strength with
310	large effect sizes. The results did not support our second hypothesis as there was no statistical difference in hip extensor
311	strength improvements between programmes. Our final hypothesis is also rejected as the programmes did not influence
312	sprint times or biomechanical measures.
313	The 4-week hamstring strengthening programmes resulted in increases in isometric and eccentric knee flexor strength
314	with strong effects, supporting similar findings in a male and female cohort after a 4 week intervention [14]. A previous
315	female specific study found that an NHE intervention required at least 6 weeks to increase eccentric hamstring strength
316	significantly [32]. This is the first study, to our knowledge, that has demonstrated the effectiveness of a shorter duration

340	 NHE programme and reported the effects of the RHC and SLHB programmes in female athletes. As isometric [7] and
341	eccentric [8] knee flexor deficits have been identified as risk factors for subsequent HSI, the results would suggest that a
342	4-week programme of different hamstring strengthening programmes may be used to address deficits identified in female
343	athletes. There were no group main effects for eccentric strength between the interventions despite NHE and RHC inter-
344	ventions resulting in greater percentage changes with moderate effect sizes in strength in the non-dominant and dominant
345	limbs compared with the SLHB intervention (NHE:12.6 and 17.5%; RHC:11.8 and 18.0%; SLHB: 1.9 and 0.1%). The NHE
346	and RHC have been described as maximal effort exercises as they require participants to eccentrically control knee exten-
347	sion (NHE) and hip and knee extension (RHC) to the point of failure during each exercise [30], generating high surface
348	EMG activity levels [33,34]. Each individual SLHB exercise in the current study was not a maximal effort exercise which
349	may generate a lower strengthening stimulus. Studies investigating the effect of short duration training interventions of 4
350	and 6 week comparing maximal versus submaximal training in untrained males found greater strength gains in the maxi-
351	mal training groups [35,36]. As it has been found that found that completing the SLHB at higher speeds and using higher
352	platforms results in greater hamstring surface EMG activity [37], further research examining the strengthening effect of
353	different SLHB effort exercises in trained, female participants is required.
354	The 4-week strengthening programmes resulted in increases in isometric hip extensor strength at 0° and 30° hip flexion
355	with strong effects bilaterally. Carmichael et al., [38] found that a 6-week isometric hip strengthening exercise programme
356	resulted in a 12% increase in isometric hip extensor strength at 0° hip flexion in recreationally active males, similar to
357	the values reported in the current study (13–20%). There was also a group main effect observed for dominant limbs for
358	isometric hip extensor strength at 0° and 30° hip flexion although post hoc analysis did not find a significant difference
359	between the groups. Given that greater trunk and gluteal isometric strength reduces HSI risk, [11] and lower concentric hip
360	extensor strength has been identified as a risk factor for HSI, [9] increasing hip extensor strength is an important consider-
361	ation in HSI prevention and rehabilitation. A 4-week programme of the NHE, SLHB or RHC may be appropriate to achieve
362	this goal in female footballers, with the NHE potentially being more practically impactful. Prospective studies comparing
363	the effects of the NHE and RHC on HSI rates in female footballers is required to fully understand the potential benefits of
364	these exercises.
365	The interventions did not affect sprint times or mechanical properties despite the increases in hip extensor and knee
366	flexor strength observed (see Table 4). This contrasts with a meta-analysis demonstrating a significant NHE-induced
367	improvement on sprint times when combined over 5, 10 and 20m distances [13]. However, a minority of the participants of
368	the total sample size were females (24/165) with only one study with a cohort solely of females [39]. Chaabone et al. [39]
369	found that an 8-week NHE programme significantly improved 5, 10 and 20m sprint times in adolescent female handball
370	players while, Amundsen et al. [32] did not observe any improvements in sprint times (5, 10, 20, 30 and 40m) in highly
371	trained, adult female soccer players following high and low volume NHE programmes over 10 weeks. The differences
372	between the results of the studies could, at least partially, be explained by the fact that the effects of NHE training on
373	sprint performance in well trained team sport players is less consistent and that a higher training intensity during the NHE
374	may be needed in well trained athletes to see benefits [13]. It is possible that the adult players were at a higher training
375	level than the adolescent population. Also, no significant correlations were found between knee flexor strength (isomet-
376	ric, isokinetic or eccentric during the NHE) and sprint times in elite female Gaelic footballers [40]. It may be that the hip
377	extensors and knee flexors contribute to sprinting in a different manner in females compared with males, a pattern that
378	has been observed in hamstring activity in lower intensity activities [41]. Also, the strength measures taken in the current
379	study were isometric or slow eccentric which may not appropriately measure the contractile properties critical for sprint
380	performance.
381	Although no statistically significant improvements in sprint performance were observed, Haugen and Buchheit [42]
382	calculated that the smallest worthwhile change (SWC) for team sport players is ~ 1.5% for 5 m sprints and~1% for 10–40
383	m sprints based upon statistical considerations of a range of appropriately powered and described studies or a 20 cm
384	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529 February 24, 2026 10 / 14
385	 increase in distance covered, based on the running speed improvement required to win a ball in football. We observed
386	smallest worthwhile changes following the NHE intervention at 5 metres and the RHC at 10 and 30 metres. For the NHE,
387	there was a decrease in performance of 1.6% (0.02 s) which corresponds to a decrease of approximately 4 cm. On the
388	other hand, the RHC intervention resulted in improved performances of 1.8% (0.04 s) and 1.2% (0.07s) in the 10m and
389	30m sprint distances respectively, corresponding to approximately 18 cm and 40 cm improvements, which may be relevant
390	in practice.
391	As there is a relationship between eccentric knee flexor strength combined with surface EMG activity and FH0 [6],
392	we hypothesised that increased knee flexor strength post intervention would lead to improved sprint mechanics. How-
393	ever, this was not the case. Previous research examining the effects of hamstring strengthening programmes have
394	reported inconsistent findings. A study on male Australian footballers found that a 14-week NHE programme resulted
395	in improved 5m and 10m sprint times, but not FH0, although there was an increase in V0 [43]. Timmins et al., [26] also
396	found that the relationship was not straightforward in a study examining the effects of a hip dominant exercise pro-
397	gramme and the NHE in addition to sprint training. They found that the NHE group improved 5m sprint times after 16
398	weeks of the intervention period only while there were no changes in mechanical sprint profiles. On the other hand,
399	there were significant increases in V0 in the flywheel group after 16 weeks, followed by a significant decrease after
400	39 weeks and an increase in increase in FH0 at end of the intervention. As the relationship between hip extensor and
401	knee flexor strengthening programmes and mechanical profiles is not clear, future research should expand the range of
402	strength variables, such as rate of torque development, [27] assessed in females to better investigate the relationship
403	with sprinting performance.
404	There are several limitations to this study. Firstly, we did not include a group without a hamstring strengthening inter-
405	vention to avoid the potential for an increased risk of injury in a group without a hamstring strengthening programme.
406	Consequently, any changes observed could therefore be due to the football training undertaken. However, we consider
407	this unlikely as 4 weeks of football training did not increase knee flexor strength in well trained soccer players [44].
408	Secondly, the NHE and RHC could be considered maximal effort exercises whereas the SLHB is not. This may have
409	resulted in a lower training stimulus with the SLHB. The SLHB was performed as initially described as deficits in this
410	measure has been previously shown to be associated with increased risk of HSI [10] and the effect of a SLHB inter-
411	vention does not seem to have been investigated. Future research should investigate the effects of adjusting the SLHB
412	exercise to increase the training stimulus. Also, although the number of participants that were initially randomised to the
413	different groups was 47, the number of participants who completed the study was 35, which did not meet the sample
414	size calculation. This will limit the generalisability of the study findings. In addition, we used clinician based resistance
415	as opposed to externally fixed resistance. Both methods have been found to have high levels of reliability although
416	differences in absolute strength measures have been found with some studies demonstrating greater strength scores
417	using externally fixed resistance compared to clinician based resistance [45,46] and others finding the opposite [47,48].
418	It is important to consider the method of strength assessment when interpreting results from the current study. Finally,
419	the strength measurements taken in this study were isometric and slow eccentric exercises. Although deficits in these
420	measurements have been identified as potential risk factors for HSIs, [7,8] they may not assess muscular properties best
421	associated with sprinting performance.
422	Conclusion
423	Elite, female Gaelic footballers demonstrated increases in knee flexor and hip extensor strength following a 4-week ham-
424	string strengthening programme of NHE, SLHB or RHC exercises with no statistical differences between the interventions.
425	As there was no group without a strengthening programme, it is not clear if the improvements were due to the interven-
426	tions or other factors, such as the regular training. There were no changes in sprint times or sprint mechanics. Longer
427	duration interventions should be considered to determine their effect on sprint performance.

Introduction
Hamstring strain injuries (HSIs) lead to a high injury burden in male and female
football with HSIs leading to 66 days and 57 absent per 1000 hours in collegiate
female and elite male Gaelic football respectively [1,2]. Approximately 60% of HSIs
occur during high speed running [3]. It is theorised that HSIs occur during terminal
swing phase when the hamstrings lengthen actively [4] as the hamstrings experi-
ence greater peak lengths and lengthening velocities. During the swing phase, the
hamstrings and gluteals produce hip extensor and knee flexor moments, acting in
a spring like fashion to slow down the forward momentum at the hip and knee [5],
with the combination of hamstrings strength and surface electromyography (EMG)
activity during late swing phase significantly contributing to horizontal ground reaction
force production [6]. The large biomechanical demands on the hamstring and gluteal
muscles indicate their importance in high speed running and performance may, at
least partially, explain the observed propensity for hamstring injury during high speed
running.
Numerous risk factors have been identified including hamstring specific issues
such as deficits in isometric, [7] eccentric, [8,9] and endurance [10] strength. Proxi-
mal risk factors have also been found; greater gluteal and trunk strength and endur-
ance [11] have been observed in those who did not sustain a HSI compared with
those who did, while lower isokinetic concentric hip extensor strength was observed
in those who subsequently sustained a HSI [9]. In terms of sprinting mechanics, low
horizontal force production during in-season testing increased HSI risk in footballers
[12]. Consequently, investigating the effects of different interventions on a range of
potential risk factors and performance outcomes are needed to refine injury preven-
tion programmes [13].
The Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) is a knee dominant hamstring exercise
found to increase hamstring eccentric strength, improve sprint times and sprint
mechanics [13]. Previous studies have demonstrated that short duration NHE
interventions of 4 weeks increase hamstring strength [14–16], fascicle length [14],
and can improve sprint times [13]. However, research is required to see if other
exercises are more effective than NHE interventions [13]. Hip dominant hamstring
muscle strengthening exercises, such as the single leg hamstring bridge (SLHB)
PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0342529 February 24, 2026 2 / 14
 leads to greater surface hamstring and gluteal surface EMG activity compared to the NHE [17], while the razor ham-
string curl (RHC) leads to greater peak eccentric knee flexor force that the NHE. [18] However, the effect of these hip
dominant exercises on HSI risk factors and sprint performance is not well understood. In addition, the majority of studies
investigating the effect of hamstring interventions have been conducted on males, with a specific need to investigate the
effects in females. [13,19] Therefore, the research question for this study was to determine the effects of three different
hamstring strengthening exercises (NHE, SLHB and RHC) on dominant and non-dominant knee flexor and hip extensor
strength measures and sprint performance in female footballers. The objectives were to assess the isometric and eccen-
tric knee flexor and isometric hip extensor strength (Newton metres per kilogramme body mass) and sprint performance
(split times, maximal horizontal force production [FH0], theoretical velocity [V0], and horizontal power output [Pmax]) before
and after a 4 week hamstring strengthening intervention and to compare the effects of the different interventions on the
strength and sprint variables. We hypothesised that
1. Participants in the 3 intervention groups would demonstrate similar improvements in knee flexor strength measures
2. Participants in the hip dominant interventions (SLHB and RHC) would demonstrate greater hip extensor gains com-
pared to the NHE
3. Participants in the 3 intervention groups would demonstrate improvements in sprint performance.
Methods
Study design
We conducted a randomised controlled trial on female Gaelic footballers from Dublin City University academy to inves-
tigate the effects of a 4-week NHE, SLHB or RHC exercise programme on knee flexor and hip extensor strength and
measures of sprint mechanics and time. The CONSORT 2010 guidelines for reporting a randomised controlled trial (S1
File) were complied with and the trial was registered (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT0573327). An a priori power anal-
ysis using G*Power 4.0 (ANOVA: repeated measures, within–between interaction; 3 groups × 5 timepoints) with f = 0.40,
α = 0.05, power = 0.80, r = 0.80, and ε = 0.75 indicated a required total sample size of 36 participants. The effect size was
informed by meta-analysis standardised mean differences for eccentric hamstring-strength adaptations (0.68–1.11)
[20,21]. Volunteers were randomised to the NHE, SLHB or RHC groups by the lead author (EW) using a 6-block randomi-
sation pattern (www.sealedenvlope.com). The NHE group were considered to be the control group given that NHE inter-
ventions have been repeatedly found to increase eccentric peak knee strength [13]. The participants or the authors who
delivered the intervention or assessed the outcomes were not blinded (AC, EH, ST, BB, JK, JT). Evaluations were per-
formed before and after the NHE, SLB and RHC programmes in the Athletic Therapy laboratory of Dublin City University.
Participants
All female collegiate Gaelic footballers (n = 342) at Dublin City University were invited to participate between the 20th of
January and 10th of February, 2023. Inclusion criteria were that participants must 18 years or older, free from hamstring
injury in the last 6 months, and currently participating in Gaelic football at a varsity level on at least 3 occasions per week.
Exclusion criteria included a history of hip or knee injury within the last 3 months, a history of anterior cruciate ligament
rupture or involvement in a hamstring strengthening programme within 3 months of the start of the study. The study was
approved by the Dublin City University Research Ethics Committee (DCUREC 2022_ATT_EW_15) and written informed
consent was provided by all participants. Participants attended two post-intervention sessions between the 27th of March
and 5th of April 2023.
A familiarisation session and two testing sessions were conducted prior to the intervention from the 13th to 24th of Feb-
ruary 2023, with each session separated by 3–5 days. Testing procedures and relevant hamstring strengthening exercises
